name: Andaman Shell Craft
tagline: Island shells turned into lamps, jewellery and gifts, under a close eye on protection.
facts: Largest craft category among the department's units, about 40
Outlet: Sagarika emporium, set up in 1960
Sales through the emporium: Rs 594.28 lakh in 2024-25
Some shells are restricted under wildlife law
art: The Industries Department describes shell crafts as one product group beside coconut shell items, wood furniture and crafts, and cane and bamboo work. Many are sold through Sagarika at fixed prices.
Details of technique, such as cutting, grinding and polishing, were not given in the sources I could read, so I have left them out.
artist: The Industries Department says the emporium began in 1960 to sell the goods made by trainees at departmental training-cum-production centres. Early sales were small, with 2-4 artisans and about Rs 8,000 a year.
In 2024-25 sales reached Rs 594.28 lakh, supporting 81 units. The peak was Rs 841.69 lakh in 2018-19. These numbers cover all products in the emporium and not only shell.

Artisans have asked for changes in the shell rules. A report on a meeting on 20 October 2021 says they asked that certain Schedule IV items be allowed in a limited and sustainable way for local artisans, and that the Union Minister said he would look into it. I found no final decision.
place: Shell craft is centred on Port Blair in South Andaman, where the government emporium Sagarika sells it. The Andaman and Nicobar Industries Department says sea shell crafts are the largest category among its assisted units, with roughly 40 registered units.
The islands have limited large industry because of their geography, and the department notes that handicrafts became a main sustainable income for many artisans.

Shell is also under law. Artisans and news reports mention that some shells are in Schedule IV of the Wild Life Protection Act, which restricts what can be used and sent out of the islands. I could not confirm the present rules, so please check with the Forest and Wildlife Department.

history.what: The Cottage Industries Emporium is set up to market goods made by trainees, later renamed Andaman and Nicobar Emporium - Sagarika.
Emporium sales peak at Rs 841.69 lakh with 56 units assisted.
On 20 October, artisans put their demands on Schedule IV shells to a Union Minister.
Sales of Rs 594.28 lakh, with 81 units assisted.

future: Training: departmental centres already teach trainees. Design and finishing training would help.
Livelihood: the emporium gives a market. Marketing outside the islands depends on the legal position on shells.
Materials: use only shells that are legal, and keep records of where they come from.
Documentation: record the artisans, techniques and shell species used, which the sources did not give.
Protection: balance artisans' income with the protection of reef shells, as the wildlife schedules aim to do.

name: Aranmula Kannadi
tagline: A mirror of polished metal, not glass, made by a few families beside the Pampa river.
facts: Medium: metal alloy, said to be copper and tin
Technique: lost-wax style casting, then days of hand polishing
Status: Geographical Indication, registered 2005
Used as: one of the auspicious items at a Kerala wedding
art: The Aranmula kannadi (kannadi means mirror) is a hand-cast metal mirror. Unlike a glass mirror, its reflecting surface is the polished metal itself, so the image has no second reflection from the back of a glass sheet.

The metal is generally described as an alloy of copper and tin, which is bronze. The exact proportions and the way it is treated are kept as a family secret, so nothing beyond this is publicly confirmed.

Reports describe casting in a clay mould in a method like lost-wax casting, followed by days of patient rubbing and polishing. Wikipedia mentions an abrasive paste of rice bran and oil from a local seed. Small pieces take a few days to finish and large ones can take months. The finished mirror is set in a decorative bronze or brass frame.
Mirrors come in many sizes, from small to large. A kannadi is counted as one of the eight auspicious items (ashtamangalyam) traditionally placed at a Kerala wedding and at other auspicious moments.
artist: The makers belong to the Viswakarma (Vishwakarma) artisan community. A well-known tale says that eight families of temple craftsmen were brought from Tamil Nadu (sources mention Tirunelveli or Sankarankovil) to work for the Aranmula temple, and settled there.
Craft families say that fewer than ten households still carry the full skill, and that making involves rituals and a vow. These figures are from a 2015 news report and may have changed.

There is a dispute over who may use the name. The Viswabrahmana Aranmula Metal Mirror Nirman Society obtained the GI; rival groups and a family trust have challenged its claim, and artisans say that copies are sold as Aranmula mirrors. We do not take a side here and do not name individual craftspeople beyond what published sources do.
Our approach: let the families describe their craft in their own words, and be clear about which mirrors are made by hand in Aranmula.
place: Aranmula is a small temple town in Pathanamthitta district, on the banks of the Pampa river, near Thiruvalla and Kozhencherry. It is low-lying, at about 7 metres above sea level.

The Aranmula Parthasarathy temple, a Krishna temple on the Pampa, is one of the 108 Vishnu temples sung of in Tamil texts. Craft legends link the mirror to the making of the temple's idol or to a crown that the artisans gave the ruler; the stories differ.

The river is also the setting of the Aranmula boat race, held on Uthrattathi in the Onam season, and of the temple feast known as the Vallasadya. These festivals bring visitors and keep the town in the public eye.
The craft lives here because of the temple, its royal patrons and a community that kept the skill within families. Artisans say cheaper imitations hurt sales.

history.what: Craftsmen from Tamil Nadu are said to have come to Aranmula to serve the temple. Some tellers say about 500 years ago; there is no firm date.
The mirror becomes a temple and royal gift, and is placed at weddings and rites.
The artisans' society applies for a Geographical Indication. IP India's record gives a registration certificate dated 19 September 2005; some sources say 2003 or 2004–05.
Artisans protest in Thiruvananthapuram and a rival group contests the GI society's claim; no ruling is reported in the sources we read.
A handful of families continue; younger members also use online sales.

future: Protect the name: a clear, shared authenticity mark so buyers can tell hand-cast Aranmula mirrors from copies.
Settle the GI dispute through a representative body that includes every genuine family.
Train young members of the families as apprentices with fair pay.
Make a visitor workshop and museum in Aranmula so tourists see the craft being made.
Flood-safe workshops and insurance for moulds, tools and stock.
Document the process as far as the families are willing, without forcing them to disclose the secret recipe.

name: Azulejo-Style Tiles of Goa
tagline: Blue and white painted tiles that came with the Portuguese and now name Goan doors.
facts: Azulejo: painted, tin-glazed tile from Iberia
Fired a second time at about 1,200 C to fix the glaze
Seen as house nameplates, on Panaji walls and in Chinchinim
Local production grew after the tiles had long been imported
art: Azulejo means a painted tile. Wikipedia says the word comes from the Arabic al-zillij, 'polished stone', and that Seville and later Portugal made azulejo a great art. In Goa the tiles carry the Portuguese tradition into village life.

A Goan workshop starts with plain ceramic tiles, about 15 cm square. A design is drawn by hand or transferred by sticker or screen print, and the colours are filled in. Bulk orders use transfers and custom pieces and murals are fully hand-painted. The tiles are glazed and fired at about 1,200 C.

Early designs were geometric and floral. Goan tiles now favour local life: fisherwomen, boats, churches and the kunbi dance. Many house nameplates are blue and white. Some tiles use caricatures in the style of the cartoonist Mario Miranda.
artist: Orlando de Noronha is credited with reviving the craft after studying in Lisbon, per Outlook Traveller. Inditales says local production began after two Goa College of Arts students studied the craft in Portugal and came back. The sources give the story differently, so we state both.

Shankar Turi, founder of Turi Azulejos in Bicholim, is named by Inditales as a maker of custom and popular designs. The Portuguese painter Jorge Colaco painted the tiles of the Menezes Braganza Hall in Panaji.
place: Azulejos can be seen at Menezes Braganza Hall in Panaji, on balconies and stairs in Panaji, and in Fontainhas, with a notable old church at Chinchinim recommended by both sources. Village houses carry nameplates.

history.what: Azulejo is thought to begin in the Arab world and travel to Spain and Portugal, per Inditales.
Portuguese azulejo develops, with its Golden Age in the 18th century, per Wikipedia.
Tiles reached Goa with the Portuguese. Inditales says they were made in Portugal and shipped, and local production started only later.
Workshops make nameplates, murals and souvenirs and run tile-painting classes.

future: Train young Goans in tile painting, glazing and firing.
Keep the hand-painted tradition alive beside quicker transfer work.
Protect old tile panels in heritage houses and public buildings.
Record the names of tile painters and their studios.
Help artisans earn from heritage tourism without losing quality.

name: Bastar Wrought Iron and Wood Carving
tagline: Iron beaten hot into animals and lamps, and timber carved into posts, doors and masks.
facts: Both crafts have GI registration (Bastar Iron Craft, item 82; Bastar Wooden Craft, item 84; 2008-09)
Iron: heated and hammered by hand
Wood: teak, rosewood and others, carved by hand
Centres: Kondagaon, Umargaon, Gunagaon and Bastar villages
art: In Bastar, iron is heated and beaten into shape. A student documentation by the National Institute of Design describes the craft as one in which iron is heated and beaten to the thickness and shape wanted, mainly by the Lohar community. Tools include hammers, chisels, tongs and a furnace. The raw material is metal sheet, long straps and coal.

Many pieces are animals: lions, deer, birds, figures in dance. Lamps with stands, lamps shaped like trees and candle stands are also made. The NID documentation says the smiths once made tools for local farmers and now also make utility and decorative goods. Gaatha adds that the smiths reuse scrap iron.

The wood carving of Bastar is tied to Adivasi life. Sahapedia lists combs, masks, tobacco boxes, musical instruments, doors, memorial posts of the Madia (khamb) and decorative panels, and notes that much of the craft is tied to Muria ghotul (youth dormitory) culture and Madia death rituals.

Wikipedia names teak, Indian rosewood and whitewood among the woods. Gaatha names Muria and Badai woodcarvers and lists geometric patterns, animals, deities and scenes of village life. The work is mostly done by hand with chisels, axes and scrapers.

Sources differ on who does which work. Wikipedia describes the Badhai as carpenters of two kinds, those who make farm tools and those who carve decorative and totemic pillars, and calls the Muria fine carvers. Sahapedia names Gond, Muria and Lohar craftspeople.
artist: These are household and village skills handed from parent to child. Wikipedia describes the iron craft as passed on through generations, and says the Gondi and Maria (Madiya) are notable among those who took up iron-smithing.

The NID documentation lists Kondagaon-area smiths including Tatiraam and Tijuraam and the brothers Ratilal, Hiralal, Nandlal and Sadanlal, who sell through boutiques, exhibitions, NGO projects and shops such as Tribes India and Bastar Arts in Raipur. We could not check their current work.
Wikipedia says Bastar artisans have won national and state awards, but we did not find a source for individual names, so none are given here.
place: Bastar is a forested district in southern Chhattisgarh, home to Gond, Abhuj Maria, Bhatra and other communities, who speak Halbi among other languages (NID documentation). Kondagaon is the centre for the crafts. It is about 73 km from Jagdalpur and about 250 km from Raipur by road.

Incredible India and Gaatha name Kondagaon, Umargaon and Gunagaon among the iron centres. Melas and Dussehra are major events in village life, and the iron and wood are bound up with the deities and festivals the NID document records.

history.what: No firm date is documented for iron-smithing or wood carving in Bastar. Wikipedia says only that the iron craft is handed down through generations.
Smiths made farm and hunting tools. Woodworkers made ritual posts, doors and everyday objects (Gaatha, Sahapedia).
Crafts reach city markets, and young people from tribal and non-tribal families take up woodcraft as a livelihood (Sahapedia).
Bastar Iron Craft (item 82) and Bastar Wooden Craft (item 84) are registered under the Geographical Indications Act, according to Wikipedia.

future: Offer apprenticeships and fair-pay orders so young Lohar and Muria artisans can stay in Bastar.
Source timber legally and sustainably, since Gaatha says deforestation is reducing good wood.
Help smiths and carvers sell directly through fairs and online, with their names on each piece.
Record the ritual objects, such as memorial posts and ghotul combs, with the community's permission, so their meanings are not lost.
Check that GI-marked goods are really made in Bastar by Bastar artisans.

name: Bidri
tagline: Silver that sings on black metal, a craft from a sultan's fort town.
facts: Medium: zinc-copper alloy, silver inlay
Process: casting, engraving, inlay, blackening
Objects: hookahs, vases, boxes, jewellery
art: Bidri ware is cast from an alloy of zinc and copper. Artisans engrave patterns, press in silver or brass wire, then rub in a paste made from special soil which turns the base metal deep black but leaves the silver bright.
Patterns include floral vines, geometric stars and Persian-influenced designs.
artist: Bidri craftsmen are mostly from Muslim artisan families, with each step done by specialists: casters, engravers and inlayers.
Shah Rashid Ahmed Quadri, a master from Bidar, received the Padma Shri in 1984 for his work in reviving the craft.
Our approach: record the full hand-chain of artisans for each piece.
place: Bidar, in the north-east corner of Karnataka, was the capital of the Bahmani sultanate in the 15th century. Its fort, Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan and tombs show a Persian-Deccani culture.
The craft's black colour famously relies on soil from the Bidar fort area.

history.what: The craft is thought to have developed in the Bahmani court, blending Persian and local metalwork traditions.
Bidri spread to Hyderabad and other Deccan courts.
A small number of families still practise; it has a geographical indication.

future: Apprenticeship fund for young artisans, as the craft is at risk of being lost.
Safer workshops: help with fume-safe casting equipment.
Contemporary design partnerships with fair credit.

name: Cane and Bamboo Craft of Arunachal
tagline: Baskets, hats, rain shields and pipes made by men from bamboo and cane.
facts: Makers: mainly men, per IGNCA
Skilled groups named: Bangni (Nyishi), Apatani, Hill Miri, Adi
Items: baskets, hats, mats, bags, pipes, ladles
Plant dyes: red, black, yellow
art: IGNCA's Janapada Sampada calls cane and bamboo work a men's craft and a major cottage industry. Items include baskets for carrying and storing paddy, fuel and water, vessels for local liquor, rice plates, bows and arrows, headgear, mats and shoulder bags.

Baskets differ by group. IGNCA describes conical carrying baskets among the Dafla, Hill Miri, Tagin, Galo, Nocte and Wancho, cylindrical grain-storing baskets among the Apatani, and flat haversack baskets among several groups.

Named items include the Apatani yatee rain shield, the bopa hat of the Apatani and Nishi decorated with a dyed hornbill beak, and the bolup hat of the Adi Galo. Apatani craftsmen also make bamboo ladles, combs and a pipe called sudhum.

Materials include bamboo species such as Dendrocalamus hamiltonii and cane from the Calamus group. Plant dyes give mainly red, black and yellow. IGNCA says the Monpa use modern paints instead and use bamboo less, mainly for basketry.
artist: The craft is mainly practised by men. Skills are learned in the family and village. I did not find named master craftsmen in the sources I read.

Down To Earth says the Apatani have managed bamboo plantations for decades and know a great deal about bamboo and cane. Their products, it says, range from houses, furniture and farm-tool handles to mats, grain baskets, beer containers, plates and spoons.
The same article says Arunachal has 26 major tribes and 105 sub-tribes and calls its bamboo and cane diversity the greatest of any Indian state. Other sources give different tribe counts.
place: The craft is spread across the state's hill communities. IGNCA names the Apatani of Ziro, the Hill Miri, the Adi of the Siang region and the Bangni (Nyishi) as the most skilled, while the Monpa and Sherdukpen use bamboo less.
Bamboo is also used to build houses in many villages. Down To Earth notes that India's Northeast holds nearly half of the country's bamboo resources.

history.what: Cane and bamboo have been used in everyday life, for houses, baskets and tools. I found no dated origin.
Cane and bamboo headgear and ritual items are held in museum collections; the National Museum records an Apatani cane headgear, per search results.
Down To Earth, in December 2025, described Apatani bamboo practice in Ziro as a living craft.

future: Training: workshops for young craftsmen in weaving, finishing and design, with elder makers as teachers.
Livelihood: develop products for city markets while keeping traditional forms, and sell through cooperatives.
Materials: support managed bamboo and cane stands, as the Apatani do.
Documentation: record local names, basket types and uses by community.
Protection: check whether any item qualifies for a Geographical Indication.

name: Chamba Metalwork
tagline: Brass and copper gods cast in lost wax, in a hill town known for its metal for a thousand years.
facts: Form: lost-wax and sand casting in brass, bronze and copper
Products: temple statues, utensils, finials (kalasha)
Age: inscribed statues name Meru Varman, early 8th century
Maker named in a 1987 study: Prakash Chand Anand
art: Chamba has a long tradition of casting and shaping metal into religious icons, household items and decorative pieces. Large relief plaques and the golden kalasha finials on temple domes are also made here.

Most statues are made by lost-wax casting. The artist builds a clay core around iron armatures, shapes a wax model, covers it in clay, melts out the wax and pours in molten metal. Small solid objects are made by sand casting. Eyes and lips are often inlaid by hand with silver or copper after casting.
A Tribune report notes the two methods: lost wax for one-of-a-kind pieces, sand casting for larger numbers. Chamba is also known for the thaal, an embossed ceremonial plate.
artist: In a 1987 Penn Museum article, Chandra Reedy describes the workshop of Prakash Chand Anand, a National Award winner for master craftsmen. She visited in 1983. He took on anyone who sincerely wished to learn, whatever their family background. Local patrons commissioned the statues for temples; the workshop also made everyday utensils to earn a living.

The Tribune (2024) quotes Ankit Verma, who continues his family's trade, and Tilak Raj Shandilya, with about 50 years of experience. They say middlemen win contracts and pass off factory goods from outside the state as local work, and that young people are leaving for better-paid jobs.
These are their statements to a newspaper, and I did not verify the specific incidents.
place: Chamba town on the Ravi was the capital of the Chamba kings from about 920 CE, by tradition. It has the Lakshmi Narayan temple complex, traditionally dated to the 10th century. Metal casting here is long established, in copper and brass.
Medieval statues in Chamba district carry inscriptions naming Meru Varman, who ruled in the early 8th century. Local copper mining reportedly ended in the 19th century when the British took control.

history.what: Large statues inscribed with the name of King Meru Varman are made.
Sahil Varman moves the capital to the site of Chamba town.
The Tribune report dates the metal craft to the reign of Sahil Verman and says Kashmiri artists brought it; other sources are less sure.
Local copper mining reportedly ends under British control.
Chandra Reedy documents the Anand workshop.
Artisans tell the Tribune of middlemen and fading patronage.

future: Training: more apprenticeships open to learners from all backgrounds, as in the Anand workshop.
Livelihood: give government and temple commissions directly to local artisans.
Materials: secure reliable supply of copper and brass at fair cost.
Documentation: record lost-wax methods and inscriptions on old statues.
Protection: authenticity marking so factory goods are not sold as Chamba work.

name: Channapatna Toys
tagline: Lacquered wooden toys, from the town that makes them.
facts: Medium: wood, often ale mara
Finish: natural lac and vegetable dyes
Technique: lathe turning
art: Channapatna toys are turned on a lathe from local wood and coated with coloured lac. Heated lac is rubbed on the spinning wood until it melts and coats, leaving a smooth, bright surface.
Toys include tops, rattles, dolls and animals. The finish is non-toxic, which makes the toys child-safe.
artist: The craft is practised by families and small workshops in Channapatna and nearby villages, and increasingly by women's groups.
Our approach: show the lathe and the lac as part of the toy's story.
place: Channapatna, between Bengaluru and Mysuru, is called 'Gombegala Ooru' ('toy town') in Kannada.
Its closeness to Bengaluru makes it a handy day trip and a growing tourist stop.

history.what: Tradition says Tipu Sultan invited artisans from Persia to teach lacquerware.
Teachers helped modernise the craft, adding new designs and dyes.
The toys have a geographical indication and face competition from plastic.

future: Sustainable wood sourcing and tree planting.
Link with schools: toys as a safe, local alternative to plastic.
New designs by young designers, with credit shared with makers.

name: Chettinad Athangudi Tiles
tagline: Colourful cement tiles poured by hand on glass, with no kiln and no electricity.
facts: Made in Athangudi village, Sivaganga district
Poured on glass, cured in water, dried in rice husk
Makers applied for a GI tag; status to be checked
Also called Chettinad or Karaikudi tiles
art: Athangudi tiles are handmade floor tiles from the Chettinad region. They are made of cement, sand and colour, not fired clay. Outlook Traveller says the process uses no electricity.

A metal stencil is set on a clean glass plate inside a mould. A slurry of cement, sand and colour is poured into the stencil. After a few minutes the stencil is lifted and the rest of the mould is filled with a dry cement-sand mix. Some makers draw designs freehand on the glass.

The tile dries for about a day and then cures in water for roughly 8 to 12 days. DT Next reports it is dried in rice husk in the sun, and says the husk oil gives a deep shine. The glass gives the face its gloss. The edges are then smoothed.
Designs are geometric and floral, often in green, blue, red and grey. Makers today also colour and shape tiles to order.
artist: Tile making is a family craft in Athangudi. The Tiles of India article names the mason Arulanantham Pillai, and says his son A. Amirthaswamy Pillai introduced fully glazed Athangudi tiles during British rule. The family firm is now run by the next generation.
Makers credit the local sand and soil for the tiles' character. Many village families work on the tiles, and each tile is laid out by hand, so no two are exactly alike.
place: Athangudi is a village in Sivaganga district in the Chettinad region of southern Tamil Nadu, near Karaikudi. The tiles are named after the village.

Chettinad is known for its large mansions of the Chettiar community, and these tiles were widely used in such houses. The Tiles of India article links the tiles to Chettiar heritage but does not name a particular sub-group.

history.what: Sources describe the craft as over 100 years old in its present form. Popular accounts call it over 500 years old; this is not supported by detailed evidence in the pages read.
A. Amirthaswamy Pillai is said to have introduced fully glazed tiles, which grew popular with locals, the English, rulers and landlords.
Makers applied for a Geographical Indication tag through the Federation of Chettinad Athangudi Heritage Flooring Tiles Manufacturers Association.
DT Next reported that the tag had not yet been granted.

future: Train young people in stencil work, colour mixing and curing.
Seek the pending GI tag, and check its status with the GI Registry.
Support the slow handmade process with fair prices, since it takes days to cure each tile.
Document traditional motifs and the families that made them.
Help conservation of old Chettinad houses so their original tiles are repaired and not replaced.

name: Coir Craft of Lakshadweep
tagline: Rope, yarn and mats from coconut husk, the islands' oldest cottage industry.
facts: Material: fibre from coconut husk
Census 2011: 7 defibering units, 6 coir yarn centres, 7 curling units
Husks were once buried in sand for about a month
Kavaratti centre: 14 women, 6 machines (PARI, 2023)
art: Coir is the fibre in the husk of a coconut. On Lakshadweep, where coconut palms are the main crop, coir is one of the main occupations alongside fishing. The People's Archive of Rural India (PARI) reports that the fibre was once drawn out by hand, spun into thread and twisted into mats, ropes and nets.
The old method was to bury husks in sand near the sea for about a month, so that they softened. The fibre was then pounded out. Most work is now done on defibering and curling machines.

PARI describes a Coir Production cum Demonstration Centre at Kavaratti, where 14 women run six machines to extract the fibre and make rope. Ropes are sold to the Coir Board in Kerala at Rs 35 a kilogram.

Some islanders say the older hand-made rope was better. PARI quotes a Kavaratti newsreader who says machine-made rope is lighter and lower in quality, and a 63-year-old fisherman from Bitra who used hand-made rope to tie his boat. These are personal views, not tested claims.
artist: PARI notes that about 80 per cent of coir workers across India are women, mostly in extraction and spinning. For Lakshadweep, the Kavaratti centre it describes is run by 14 women.
They work eight-hour shifts, Monday to Saturday, and earn about Rs 7,700 a month, according to PARI in 2023. Half of each shift is rope making and half is cleaning the machines.
I did not find the names of individual hand-spinners or master rope makers.
place: Lakshadweep is a string of coral islands in the Arabian Sea. Coconut palms cover most of the dry land, which is why husk is so plentiful. The Census of 2011 recorded seven coconut defibering units, six coir yarn production centres and seven fibre curling units in the territory.
Fishing boats were also tied and rigged with coir rope, and Young INTACH describes the odam as built from coconut wood and coir.

history.what: Coir was extracted by hand, buried in sand to ret, then pounded and spun into thread, then twisted into ropes, mats and nets.
Defibering and curling machines took over fibre extraction, as PARI describes.
Census records seven defibering units, six yarn centres and seven curling units in the territory.
PARI reports the Kavaratti demonstration centre, with women selling rope to the Coir Board at Rs 35 a kilogram.

future: Pay fair rates for rope, so that a day of coir work gives a living wage.
Teach and record the old hand-spinning methods with the senior women who still know them.
Add value locally with mats, yarn and craft goods, so that not all rope leaves as raw rope.
Test and publish how well hand-made and machine-made rope perform, so that opinions can be checked.
Find out how much husk goes unused and whether more could be processed.

name: Dhodia Bamboo Craft
states: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
tagline: Baskets and mats woven from bamboo in the forest villages around Silvassa.
facts: Craft: woven bamboo baskets and mats
Basket-making is called the most popular bamboo craft of the territory
Dhodia are one of the main tribes of the territory
Sources I read do not tie bamboo work to the Dhodia alone
art: Bamboo basketry is a living craft of Dadra and Nagar Haveli. A craft map by INTACH's Young INTACH programme calls basket making the most popular bamboo craft of the territory. Baskets run from small carriers to large storage baskets, and are traditionally woven from a flexible bamboo it names gaoghari vaas.
The same page names some forms: the chhabdi, a shallow dish for food; the moti topli, a large storage basket; and the karandia, a bamboo house for chickens.
Incredible India says tribal artisans also weave mats from bamboo twigs and cane, which it calls palas. Another site says the mats carry traditional motifs but does not describe them.

Important caution: I found no source that says bamboo craft belongs to the Dhodia in particular. Official pages list the Dhodia among the territory's main tribes, alongside the Varli, Kokna and Kathodi. The name of this entry follows the project brief, and the craft itself should be read as a craft of the forest tribes of the territory.
artist: The makers are tribal families of the territory. Official sources name the Varli, Dhodia, Kokna, Kathodia, Dubla, Naika and Koli among the communities
I could not find named master weavers, or any source that says which community makes which form, so I have not assigned the craft to one tribe.
place: Dadra and Nagar Haveli is a small territory of forest, farm and river land inland from the Gujarat coast. Silvassa, the capital, is where baskets and mats are sold as souvenirs, and the National Tribal Art and Food Festival is held there each year from 1 to 7 May, according to Incredible India.

Bamboo grows in the forests of the region, and the baskets are made for farm and household use as well as sale. The Silvassa Tribal Museum shows the tools and household goods of the Varli, Dhodia, Kokna and Kathodia tribes.

history.what: Sources describe basket making as a traditional craft but give no founding date.
Incredible India presents mats and baskets as popular souvenirs sold in Silvassa and at its yearly tribal festival.

future: Document which families weave which forms, so that the Dhodia and other communities are credited correctly.
Train young weavers in design and finishing, so that baskets and mats can find city buyers.
Plan bamboo supply with the forest department so that families have steady access to good, sustainably cut bamboo.
Seek a Geographical Indication or craft mark only if the weavers themselves want it.
Put the weaver's name and village on each product sold in Silvassa.

name: Etikoppaka Toys
tagline: Soft ankudu wood, turned on a lathe and sealed with lacquer coloured by seeds, bark and leaves.
facts: Craft: turned wood with lacquer colouring
Wood: ankudu (Wrightia tinctoria)
Colours: natural dyes from seeds, resin, bark, roots and leaves
Geographical Indication granted in 2017
art: Etikoppaka is known as the toy village. Artisans there make spinning tops, rattles, animal figures, dolls and boxes for jewellery and vermilion. The toys are rounded and brightly coloured, and the process is described as safe for children.

The wood is ankudu (Wrightia tinctoria), a soft, light wood. The craft is called turned wood lacquer work. A piece of wood is spun on a lathe and a stick of coloured lacquer is held against it. One account says the friction melts the lacquer so that it spreads smoothly over the wood.

The colours come from natural dyes made from seeds, resin, bark, roots and leaves. One trade source says that before about 1910 the reds came mainly from the divi-divi tree, but I found this in only one place.

Toys have long been part of family life. Wikipedia notes that a girl was given a miniature kitchen set, called lakkapidathalu, on her first birthday, and that toys carrying turmeric, kumkum and betel nuts went into a bride's trousseau. Families also display them during Bommala Koluvu, the doll festival.
artist: Men traditionally made the toys, and women helped at home. WIPO reports that as many men moved to better paid city work, women formed groups, learned woodworking and now make the toys with help from experienced local artisans.

WIPO says about 140 women artisans in and around Etikoppaka are supported by cooperatives. Some have taken loans to set up production, buy machines and rent workspace. Their income goes to food and schooling for their children.
I could not verify the names of individual master artisans from the pages I read, so none are named here.
place: Etikoppaka is a small village on the bank of the Varaha River in Anakapalli district, in north coastal Andhra Pradesh. Older writing places it in Visakhapatnam district. Telugu is the language of the village.

Wikipedia says toys were once sold at country fairs, weekly markets, railway stations and bus stands. Today they also go to cities and abroad, and Wikipedia lists the USA, Australia, France, Italy and Germany among the export markets.

history.what: Sources describe the craft as 300 to 400 years old. These are popular estimates, not documented dates.
One account says artisans from Nakkapalli, about 25 km away, moved to Etikoppaka because ankudu wood grew in the nearby forests. I read this only in a search summary, so treat it with care.
The toys received a Geographical Indication tag. WIPO says the Andhra Pradesh Handicrafts Development Corporation led the effort.

Wikipedia says the tag helped reduce counterfeiting and raise sales. It also lists awards from the National Innovation Foundation and UNESCO's Seal of Excellence for Handicrafts, which I did not check against the awarding bodies.

future: Offer women's groups steady training in lathe work, design and accounts.
Help artisans buy ankudu wood at fair prices. WIPO notes that women are asking for subsidies on wood.
Support the natural dye process by keeping records of dye plants and recipes, and by paying growers and collectors fairly.
Teach artisans what a GI means and how to use it, since WIPO says many know little about IP rights.
Build direct selling channels so the maker, and not only the trader, keeps the profit.

name: Firozabad Glass
tagline: The glass bangle town near Agra, where furnaces burn at about 1,200 degrees.
facts: Main product: glass bangles, plus tableware and lab glass
Furnaces burn at about 1,200 C
Bangles: about 46 per cent of national production (Wikipedia)
Origin of the trade: sources differ
art: Firozabad is the main glass-making town of India and its largest source of glass bangles. Bangles, chandeliers, lab glassware, tableware and decorative pieces are made there.

Outlook Traveller describes the bangle method. Recycled glass is mixed with sand, soda, chemicals and colour, then melted in furnaces at about 1,200 degrees Celsius. Workers called gulliwalas carry the molten glass on long metal pipes to the artisans. The artisans wrap the glass around an iron rod called a muttha and spin it on a motor to form coils, and one muttha can yield around 368 bangles. Broken pieces go back in the furnace.
The older way was slower. Each bangle was made one at a time by shaping gathered molten glass on a turning stone cone called a kalbhut.
artist: The Omeka exhibit on Firozabad's bangle industry says the first bangle makers were the Manihars, a Muslim caste of bangle sellers, who later took the title Sheeshgarh. It records Rustam Ustad, a Sheeshgarh master craftsman who died in 1947 and is credited locally with the invention of the craft. Treat that as local tradition.

Wikipedia says bangle making employed about 100,000 people in 2011, and describes poor conditions: long hours, heat illness, dust and noise, and child labour. A 1986 report estimated nearly 50,000 children under 14 worked in glass production. These are old figures and I do not have a current count.

Outlook Traveller notes that bangle demand has fallen to about a fifth of its early-1980s level, and that the change from wood and coal furnaces to natural gas, made to cut pollution, closed many businesses.
place: Firozabad is a city in Uttar Pradesh about 40 to 44 km from Agra, near the Yamuna, at about 27.16 N, 78.39 E. Wikipedia says the modern city was founded around 1566 under Akbar. It adds that the older settlement was Chandwar, a Chauhan Rajput stronghold.

The industry is clustered in the town. Outlook Traveller counts about 400 registered glass units, and the main bazaar sells bangles to visitors. Wikipedia says Firozabad produces about 70 per cent of the country's unorganised-sector glass output, with an estimated 35 to 50 per cent exported.
These figures come from encyclopaedic and travel writing, not from an official census, so they are estimates.

history.what: Outlook Traveller says the trade began when locals melted discarded glass left by the Mughals in furnaces called bhainsa bhatti, first making bangles and small bottles. Another source says Akbar set up a glass factory here. I could not confirm either from a primary source.
Industrial bangle production from Bohemia, in today's Czech Republic, threatens the hand craft, according to the Omeka exhibit.

Indian industrialists set up industrial estates in Firozabad to counter imported bangles, hiring foreign specialists. The exhibit names an Austrian blower, Mozina, who supervised the largest factory, and a Japanese expert who helped design cheap furnaces.
The Bohemian bangle industry declines, and Firozabad becomes the only major glass-bangle centre (Omeka exhibit).
Bangle demand falls to about a fifth of its early-1980s level (Outlook Traveller).
Pollution rules push furnaces to natural gas, and many small units close.

future: Training: teach furnace and coil-making skills in safe conditions, and keep schooling for workers' children.
Livelihood: new products such as decorative glass and gifts, since bangle demand is falling.
Materials: cleaner, safer furnaces with support for small units to switch fuel.
Documentation: record the Manihar and Sheeshgarh craft families and the old kalbhut method.
Protection: enforce rules against child labour and improve heat, dust and noise protection.

name: Goan Clay Pottery
tagline: Wheel-thrown pots from the kumbhar potters, now a craft of very few hands.
facts: Made by the Kumbhar potter community
Traditional pots were used for cooking
Potters also make the body of the ghumot drum
Most potters now use motor-driven wheels
art: Goan clay pots were made for the kitchen and the home. A photo essay on goa.me says traditional Goan pots were once used for cooking and are now mostly bought as home decor.
The potter shapes the clay on a wheel. In the essay, a potter at Sarzora uses a traditional hand-driven cart wheel, while most other Goan potters now use motor-driven wheels.
Potters also make the earthen body of the ghumot, Goa's pot drum. Wikipedia says traditional potters make the body, and the skin is stretched over it.
Our sources did not describe clay sources, firing or decoration, so we do not describe them. This entry is short for that reason.
artist: Pottery is the work of the Kumbhar community. The goa.me essay by Rahul Nair follows Zuanvar Fernandes of Sarzora, who at the time of writing was 84. He began learning from his grandfather at the age of six and is reported to be the only Kumbhar left in his village. Each afternoon he prepares clay for the next day, and he sells to local shops in Madgaon and Navelim.
A Down To Earth article on the ghumot says the community of makers is shrinking, and some have adapted to new materials.
place: Sarzora, in South Goa, was once famous for pottery. Fernandes sells in Madgaon and Navelim nearby.
Other pottery centres exist in Goa, but we could not open the pages that name them, so we do not list them.

history.what: Fernandes learned from his grandfather, so the family craft runs back at least two generations in this account.
Use of pots for cooking has fallen. Most buyers now use them as decor. Motor wheels have replaced hand-driven ones for most potters.
The Government of Goa declared the ghumot, made without monitor lizard skin, a state heritage instrument.

future: Document the remaining Kumbhar families and their methods in their own words.
Support apprenticeships so a village does not lose its last potter.
Help potters sell directly through craft fairs and shops.
Link pottery with ghumot making, so drum makers and players work together.
Secure clay access and workshop space for potters.

name: Handmade Paper of Puducherry
tagline: Cotton-rag paper made by hand at the Sri Aurobindo Ashram since 1959.
facts: Unit set up in 1959 (Sahapedia)
Main input: cotton rag waste from Tirupur textile mills
Marbled paper inspired by Japanese suminagashi
Located in Puducherry, north of the Boulevard
art: The Sri Aurobindo Ashram runs a handmade paper factory in Puducherry. Sahapedia's craft walk says it was set up in 1959 in a coconut plantation north of the Boulevard. A travel guide also gives 1959 and says it was founded under the inspiration of The Mother, the Ashram's spiritual head.

Sahapedia reports that the main input is white cotton rag waste from textile factories in Tirupur. The factory also uses bio-based fibres such as bamboo, pineapple, eucalyptus leaves, banana and sugarcane fibre, straw and husk.

The paper is marbled using a technique inspired by the Japanese suminagashi. Sahapedia says the Ashram first tried this in 1942 and that each sheet is unique. Products include stationery, journals and art papers sold in the factory shop, according to the travel guide.
The entry name mentions Auroville. I found no reliable page that links Auroville to this factory, so this entry is about the Ashram's paper unit.
artist: The workers are Ashram members and employees who carry out each step, from preparing rag to pressing and drying. The travel guide mentions skilled artisans but not their numbers.

I found no named paper makers in the sources I could read. This unit sits within the Ashram's work-as-practice approach, as the travel guide puts it, which combines labour with the community's spiritual life.
place: Puducherry is a former French settlement on the Coromandel Coast. The Ashram, founded by Sri Aurobindo and The Mother, is at the heart of the old town, and its activities include several workshops.
The paper factory stands on the north side of the Boulevard, once a coconut plantation. The pin is approximate.

history.what: According to Sahapedia, the Ashram first tried marbling paper in a way inspired by suminagashi.
The handmade paper unit was set up, per Sahapedia and a travel guide. Other accounts may differ; I use 1959.
Sahapedia describes the unit's use of rag waste and plant fibres. Tours and workshops are offered, according to the travel guide.

future: Keep buying rag waste from textile mills so that it is reused and not discarded.
Document the marbling method and train more people in it.
Offer paper-making courses for schools and visitors.
Test more plant fibres, such as banana and sugarcane waste, so as to cut the use of virgin pulp.
Tell the story of the paper makers by name on the products.

pins.label: Sri Aurobindo Ashram handmade paper factory

name: Haryana Terracotta
tagline: Jhajjar's clay water pitchers and the village potter's wheel of Haryana.
facts: Form: fired clay (terracotta) pottery
Best known: surahi water pitchers of Jhajjar
A GI application for Jhajjar Pottery was filed in October 2025
Status of that application: pre-examination
art: Pottery is described by Indianetzone as a village craft in Haryana, from everyday pots to decorative pieces. The craft depends on naturally available clay.

Clay water pitchers are a main product. Indianetzone says the pitchers of Jhajjar are in great demand and are reported to make water taste sweeter. That is a local belief reported by the source, not a tested claim.
The sources I could open do not describe the potter's tools, firing method or decoration in detail, so this entry stays short.
artist: The sources I read do not name individual potters, so none are named here.

The India Patent Office record of GI application 1653 shows the applicant is the Rural and Urban Development Foundation of Bahadurgarh, Jhajjar. The record lists supporting documents on the history, method and the potter families, but I could not read their contents.
place: Indianetzone names Gurgaon, Jhajjar, Faridabad and Kurukshetra as notable centres of terracotta work in Haryana, and Jhajjar as the best-known for water pitchers.
Jhajjar town lies west of Delhi in the plains of Haryana.

history.what: Indianetzone treats pottery as an old village craft of Haryana. I found no source here that dates its origins.
The Rural and Urban Development Foundation files a GI application for Jhajjar Pottery of Haryana, under handicrafts.
The applicant replies to the formality check report. The status is listed as pre-examination. It is not a registered GI.

future: Protection: the GI application, if granted, could help protect the Jhajjar name. It is not yet granted.
Livelihood: help potters sell to hotels and homes in the Delhi region and keep prices fair in the cooler months.
Documentation: survey the potter families, clay sources and kilns, and record the work of each.
Training: teach young potters new forms and glazes while keeping the traditional pitcher.

name: Hodi (Nicobarese Canoes)
tagline: The outrigger canoe of the Nicobar Islands, built by community knowledge and raced at festivals.
facts: Type: outrigger canoe
Registered with a GI tag: Nicobari Hodi, Registration No. 998
GI applicant: Tribal Development Council, Andaman and Nicobar Islands
Used for fishing, transport and races
art: The hodi is an outrigger canoe. Next IAS, summarising the GI application, says builders use knowledge passed down by the Nicobarese and that designs vary slightly from island to island. Wood comes from local trees or from nearby islands. It does not name the species.
The hodi is not only a boat. A tuhet, a group of families under a headman, considers it an asset, the same source says. The canoe is also part of ceremony and sport, as in the Pig Festival races.
Details of carved canoe decoration were not available in the sources I could read, so they are left out.
artist: The sources I read do not name individual boat builders. The skill is described as community knowledge held by the Nicobarese.
The Tribal Development Council of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands applied for the GI tag. News reports from 2022 call it the first GI application from the Union Territory.

Nicobar Times reported on 6 December 2024 that seven products of the islands received GI tags, including the Nicobari Hodi (Registration No. 998). Other products in that list are the Nicobari Mat, Nicobari Hut, Padauk Wood Craft, Andaman and Nicobar Coconut, Nicobari Virgin Coconut Oil and Andaman Karen Musley Rice.
place: The hodi is used across the Nicobar group. A Nicobar Times report on the 2026 World Heritage tentative-list entry says the hodi was a key tool for fishing, transport and inter-island trade in the Central group, also called the Nancowrie group. That group covers Trinket, Katchal, Chowra, Teressa, Kamorta, Nancowrie and Bompoka.
The same report calls the Chowra canoe, the ap, one of the island's most symbolic features.
The annual Panuohonot, or Pig Festival, includes pig fighting, hodi canoe races, wrestling, music and dance, the report says. Races are held between islands and villages.

history.what: The Tribal Development Council applies to the GI Registry in Chennai for the Nicobari Hodi.
Nicobar Times reports the GI grant, Registration No. 998.
The Central Nicobar cultural landscape, including the hodi and the Pig Festival, is submitted for India's World Heritage tentative list by the Archaeological Survey of India.

future: Training: record who still builds the hodi and bring young people into the work.
Livelihood: GI use should benefit the builders themselves, with clear rules on who may use the name.
Materials: record which trees are used and how they are sourced, as the sources do not say.
Documentation: make a community-led record of the building steps and the terms for each part of the canoe.
Protection: keep the canoe races and festivals alive, as they give the craft a purpose.

pins.label: Chowra, home of the ap canoe

name: Jaipur Blue Pottery
tagline: Pottery made without clay, painted in cobalt blue and fired once.
facts: No clay: quartz powder, powdered glass, multani mitti and gum
Fired once at low temperature
Colours: cobalt blue, copper green, white
Has a Geographical Indication tag
art: Despite the name, Jaipur blue pottery uses no clay. Wikipedia says the dough is made from quartz powder, powdered glass, multani mitti (fuller's earth), borax, gum and water. The dough is rolled out and pressed into plaster moulds.

After drying, the piece is sanded, painted by hand while it is turned, glazed, and fired once at a low temperature for about four to five hours. The kiln then takes two to three days to cool. The ware is fragile but can be used daily.

The palette is mainly cobalt blue, copper green and white, with a little yellow or brown. Motifs include birds, animals, flowers, Mughal arabesques, light Persian geometry and Hindu deities. Typical objects are vases, plates, bowls, tiles and door knobs, and today also beads and pendants.
Makers have moved to lead-free glazes and diesel furnaces, according to Wikipedia.
artist: Blue pottery today is made by workshop teams: those who prepare the dough, mould, paint, glaze and fire. Most of them go unnamed in the writing we read.

Two names recur in the story of the revival. Kripal Singh Shekhawat, a painter and muralist who led the ceramics department of the Jaipur art school, is called the modern father of the craft by Homegrown. Leela Bordia, who began working with struggling artisans in 1978, is credited by 30 Stades with widening the products into beads and jewellery and winning foreign orders; her firm Neerja International is described there as the largest maker and exporter.
Wikipedia and 30 Stades also name the patrons Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay and Maharani Gayatri Devi.
place: Jaipur is the centre of the craft, with Sanganer, Mahalan and Neota also named as production areas by Wikipedia. Jaipur's own makers work in workshops across the city.
The craft is linked to the city's palaces, museums and the Jaipur school of art, which Sawai Ram Singh II founded in 1866 according to 30 Stades, and later to the Sawai Ram Singh Shilp Kala Kendra.

history.what: Wikipedia traces blue-and-white ware to Abbasid Iraq, then through China, Persia and Central Asia, reaching India with Turkic and Mughal rule. Homegrown links it to Mongol and Mughal craftspeople and Kashmir. Accounts differ.

history.when: Sawai Ram Singh II (reigned 1835-1880 per Wikipedia; 1830-1885 per 30 Stades)
history.what: He is credited with bringing the craft to Jaipur. A popular story says it began when kite-flying potters, Churamani and Kaluram from Achnera near Agra, were invited to teach at the art school. 30 Stades calls this a report, and it should be treated as legend.
Jaipur School of Art founded, according to 30 Stades.
The craft had nearly disappeared. Homegrown says master potters would not share their knowledge.
Kripal Singh Shekhawat revived it with help from Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay and Gayatri Devi. The Shilp Kala Kendra was founded in 1963 (30 Stades). Sources differ on exact years.
Leela Bordia began working with artisans and expanded the range of products (30 Stades).
Jaipur Blue Pottery has a GI tag. Our sources give 2009 (30 Stades) and 2006 (a search summary), so we do not give a year.

future: Train young painters and moulders inside workshops, with fair apprenticeship pay.
Keep the lead-free glaze and cleaner kiln work going, with support for the cost of change.
Use the GI tag to separate genuine blue pottery from imitation ceramics.
Keep an open record of motifs, recipes and makers, with each workshop's name.
Widen the market beyond tourism, such as tiles and architecture, so that artisans have steady work.

name: Japi
tagline: A cone of bamboo and tokou leaf that shades a farmer and honours a guest.
facts: Conical hat of bamboo or cane and tokou paat (palm leaf)
Names from jaap, a bundle of tokou leaves
Plain for work, ornate for ceremony
Assam Jaapi received a GI tag in March 2024
art: The japi, also spelled jaapi, is a conical hat from Assam. Wikipedia describes it as made of tightly woven bamboo or cane and tokou paat, a large palm leaf. The name comes from jaap, a bundle of tokou leaves.

There are many kinds. Wikipedia lists the sorudoi, worn by women, especially brides; the bordoi, for royalty; the panidoi or haluwa, for field farmers; the garakhiya, for cattle herders; the pitha, a hood; and the tupi or varun, a rain hat. A plain japi protects the worker from sun and rain. A decorated one is a mark of status and respect.
Today it is also a symbol of Assam. Wikipedia says it is worn during Bihu dance, offered as a sign of respect and hung as a welcome decoration. WION describes it as a symbol of respect in Assam.
artist: Japi makers are mostly village families who split bamboo, weave the frame, stitch tokou leaves and add cloth or woven borders. We could not find a reliable source that names the process step by step, so this page does not.
Wikipedia says that under Ahom rule the Sutiya (Chutia) people controlled the japi-making guild.
place: Japi is made and used across the Brahmaputra valley. We could not confirm the main production districts from a page we opened, so none are named here.
In the rainy paddy fields of Assam, the broad cone is a practical thing: it keeps rain off the neck and shades the face.

history.what: Wikipedia says the last Sutiya king gave gold and silver japis to Ahom king Suhungmung in an attempt at a treaty.
Sutiya kings used the japi as a cultural symbol; under the Ahoms the Sutiyas controlled the japi-making guild.
The Chief Minister announced a GI tag for Assam Jaapi, among six Assam crafts.

future: Training: workshops for young weavers in bamboo splitting and leaf stitching.
Livelihood: sell plain working japis as well as decorative ones, with fair prices for the makers.
Materials: protect bamboo and tokou leaf supply through community growing.
Protection: use the GI tag to separate hand-made japis from factory copies.
Documentation: record each regional type and its makers by name.

name: Kallai Mats
tagline: Woven island mats from leaf and fibre; the local name kallai could not be confirmed.
facts: Materials named for Lakshadweep: coir and screw pine leaves
The name kallai did not appear in any source I read
Weavers also make baskets
Short entry: sources are thin
art: This is a short entry. I could not find any source that uses the name kallai for a mat, or one that describes a mat tradition on a particular island by that name. The brief gave the name, and I record that I could not verify it.

What the sources say is general. Young INTACH writes that Lakshadweep weavers make mats and baskets from coir, the fibre from coconut husk, and from screw pine leaves. It does not name particular mat types.
I did not find how the leaves are prepared or woven on the islands.
artist: I found no named weavers, cooperatives or islands in the sources I read, and none that say who weaves the mats.
place: Lakshadweep is a set of coral islands in the Arabian Sea, with palms, sand and little farm land. Coconut husk and screw pine are among the few local materials, which is why mats and baskets from them are a natural craft there.
The pins show Kavaratti, the capital, and Kalpeni. They do not mark proven mat-making sites.

history.what: I found no dated history of mat weaving in Lakshadweep.
Young INTACH describes the machhwa, a lagoon boat with a mat sail, which shows mats were used in island life beyond the floor.
PARI reports the long link between coir and island livelihoods, and the later shift to machines.

future: Interview island women to find out what mats they weave, what each is called, and whether kallai is a local word.
Record patterns and methods on video with the weavers' own names for them.
Check the supply of screw pine and husk so the craft is not held back by materials.
Link weavers to buyers through the territory's handicraft outlets, with a fair price.
Consider a craft mark or GI only if weavers want one and can show the proof.

name: Karaikal Terracotta
tagline: Clay horses, elephants and toys from the potters of the Puducherry territory.
facts: Potters of the Kulalar community make GI-tagged terracotta at Villianur
Karaikal itself: I found no source describing its terracotta
Villianur terracotta was registered as a GI in 2011
Short entry: only regional sources found
art: This is a short entry. I found no page that describes terracotta work in Karaikal. Karaikal is one of the four parts of the Puducherry territory, and the documented terracotta of the territory is centred on Villianur, near Puducherry town.

Wikipedia says Villianur terracotta is made from green clay, fine sand and a river clay called thennal. The clay is sifted, mixed roughly 20 per cent clay, 40 per cent thennal and 40 per cent sand, then moulded or shaped by hand, dried for about 12 hours and fired for about 30 minutes with husk and powdered wood.

Products include Ayyanar horses, elephants, Ganesha figures and household items. One horse is six feet tall with removable parts. Sahapedia notes that earthenware is still sold on the potters' street, Kosakadai street, in the Tamil town of Puducherry.

The Puducherry industries department describes terracotta toys of deities, animals, birds, fruits and vegetables, made by local craftsmen and priced from Rs 10 to Rs 10,000. It does not mention Karaikal.
artist: Sahapedia and Wikipedia name the Kulalar, the potter community, as makers of Villianur terracotta. Wikipedia says the tradition is over 20 generations old.

A master craftsman named in several sources is V.K. Munusamy of Villianur. Outlook Traveller calls him a Padma Shri awardee of 2020, and Wikipedia reports a UNESCO award in 2005. I did not check these honours against an official list.
I found no named potters from Karaikal.
place: Karaikal is a port town on the Coromandel Coast, in the fertile Kaveri delta, and an enclave surrounded by Tamil Nadu. The French held it from 1739, with a British period from 1760 to 1817, until 1954.

Terracotta shrines of Ayyanar, the village guardian, with clay horses are common across Tamil country, and potters work in delta villages. I did not find a source tying this to Karaikal, so I mark the pins as approximate.

history.what: The Puducherry industries department notes terracotta toys excavated at Arikamedu, near Puducherry.
Wikipedia says the Villianur art form received a boost under French rule. Karaikal was French from 1739, with a break of British control.
Karaikal was de facto incorporated into India, per Wikipedia, and de jure in 1962.
Villianur terracotta works were registered as a Geographical Indication, per Wikipedia.

future: Survey Karaikal's potters and kilns, to learn what is made there and by whom.
Record potters' own accounts of what they make and for whom.
Help potters get good clay and fuel at fair prices.
Teach young people the full craft, and offer visitors workshops with potters paid for their time.
Check whether the GI registration could cover potters elsewhere in the territory.

name: Kashmiri Papier-Mâché
tagline: Paper pulp turned into lacquered, gilded treasures.
facts: Medium: paper pulp, lacquer
Stages: sakhtsazi (making) and naqashi (painting)
Objects: boxes, vases, trays, ornaments
art: Kashmiri papier-mâché begins with pulped paper, moulded into boxes, bowls and ornaments, dried, then sealed and painted. The painted surface is decorated with flowers, vines, birds and, often, gold, then lacquered.
The designs, such as chinar leaves, irises and Persian-style floral patterns, show the valley's landscape and its links to Central Asia.
artist: The craft has two roles: sakhtsazi, who make the object, and naqash, who paint it. Painters train for years and some designs are held in family notebooks.
Our approach: credit both the maker and the painter.
place: Srinagar's old city, along the Jhelum river, is home to workshops. The Dal Lake and mountains provide the images.
Kashmir's climate, cold winters, shaped a culture of indoor crafts.

history.what: The craft is said to have come to Kashmir from Persia and Central Asia.
It grew under local rulers and found markets in Europe.
Tourism is a major market, but disruptions and the 2014 floods have hurt the trade.

future: Keep painters paying their way by finding direct buyers.
Train young painters and record their patterns.
Rebuild flood-damaged workshops and stock.
