name: Kauna Craft
tagline: Mats and baskets woven from a wetland grass, from household floors to city handbags.
facts: Material: kauna grass, grown by farmers
Traditional item: the phak, a floor mat
Women are more prominent in the craft; men also weave
New products: totes, clutches, table mats, hats
art: Kauna is a grass used for weaving in Manipur. According to the Google Arts and Culture story on the craft, farmers grow it, and the stem is also eaten as food. Weavers work it by hand. Some pieces are shaped over a mould and smaller items are made freehand.

The grass can be woven in its natural tone or dyed, with industrial or natural colours. Patterns come from colour or from the layout of the weave. Looser weaves suit baskets that carry bulky items and need airflow. Finer weaves are strengthened with extra strips.

The traditional products are phak floor mats and mattresses, cushions, and storage and laundry baskets. The mats are the most widely used, and finer designs are used for weddings and ceremonies. Newer products include tote and shopping bags, handbags with tassels, clutches, table mats, hats and wall clocks.
artist: The story names several makers. Takhellie Sundrei, called Ima Yai in her community, runs production in Tulel Khun village and supports other workers. Nityai Moirangthem is a basket weaver known for strong clasps and varied textures. Akhom Raso Singh of Akhom Handicrafts makes wall clocks and mats. Becha Irangbom of Eta Kauna Handicraft in Imphal makes embroidered bags. The Women's Income Generation Centre in Thoubal is another production group.
Women are more prominent in the craft, especially when men work outside the home, but men and women both take part.
place: The story places the craft in Manipur, including Tulel Khun village, the Wangkhei area of Imphal, and Thoubal. The Handicrafts Department of India describes kauna grass as grown in Imphal's wetlands and traditionally used by the Meitei for hats, baskets and hampers. We did not find a source that ties kauna to Loktak Lake or to Moirang, so this entry does not claim it.

history.what: Kauna items were first made for everyday household use. Coloured pieces were used as ceremonial gifts.
Designs stayed limited until producers began serving urban customers with more refined tastes, and training workshops encouraged them to diversify.
Weavers work with grass farmers and local entrepreneurs. Samples go to retailers across India and abroad, and natural-coloured baskets are shipped in bulk through exporters.

future: Training: more design and finishing workshops, especially for young weavers.
Livelihood: fair prices for weavers and farmers, and direct links to buyers so more money stays with makers.
Materials: protect the wetlands where the grass grows, and support farmers who grow it.
Documentation: record the named weaves and the stories of the makers.
Protection: check the craft's registration status with the GI registry before claiming any GI tag; sources we found disagree.

name: Khasi and Garo Cane and Bamboo Craft
tagline: Rain shields, pig baskets and fish traps woven from the cane and bamboo of the hills.
facts: Practised by Khasi, Garo and Jaintia communities
A GlobalInch craft page ranks it second to agriculture in the state economy
Famous piece: the knup, the Khasi rain shield
Techniques include coiling, double-walled weaving and pokerwork
art: Cane and bamboo work is part of daily life across Meghalaya. A craft profile on GlobalInch lists khoh carrying baskets, Khasi pig-packing baskets, winnowing fans, mats, low stools, fish traps, combs and pipes. It also lists the knup, a rain shield worn on the back, and a wide-brimmed bamboo and cloth hat for Khasi women. Garo artisans are noted for decorative meghum khoks baskets and shields.

The techniques are varied. The page names open-hexagonal, twill and spiral weaves. Double-walled baskets are made by weaving one layer over the other. Whole cane is coiled and bound with split cane, as in the nesting containers sold in Shillong. Palm leaves are sandwiched between woven layers to make them waterproof. Designs can also be burned into bamboo with a heated rod, which the page calls pokerwork.

The materials are local. The page names bamboo species such as Ryngngai, used for construction, Trylaw for paper making and Tyr-a for fences and walls. Cane includes Rimet and Riphin. Thread, resin for fixing comb teeth and soft wood for handles are also used.
artist: The craft is shared by the three hill communities, the Khasi, Garo and Jaintia. The GlobalInch page says artisans usually do this work when they are not farming. Products fall into two groups: everyday items for local use, and finer decorative pieces for wider markets.

I did not find named master craftspeople in the sources I read. Producer groups exist, such as the women-led Laidlang self-help group, which appeared in a search result listing, but I did not open that page.
place: The Khasi Hills, Garo Hills and Jaintia Hills are rich in bamboo and cane. Shillong is the main place visitors buy the finished work, with coiled cane containers and other pieces sold there.
The GlobalInch page notes that taking bamboo out of the Garo Hills is hard and needs experienced workers. Transport of materials and products is also a problem.

history.what: The sources I read give no dated history. They describe the crafts as part of the creative traditions of the hill communities.
Many forms, like the knup rain shield, pig baskets and fish traps, grew from farming and hill life.
The craft is described as the state's second-largest economic activity after agriculture.

future: Training: apprenticeships with experienced cutters and weavers, especially for hard work like extracting bamboo in the Garo Hills.
Livelihood: the page names capital as the most important difficulty. Small loans and group buying could help artisans.
Materials: bamboo and cane stocks need careful harvest so the supply lasts.
Documentation: a record of local product names, such as knup, tlieng and meghum khoks, and of makers by village would help.
Protection: roads and fair markets would help artisans reach buyers without losing price to middlemen.

name: Khurja Pottery
tagline: Glazed ceramics with floral borders from the 'Ceramic City' of Bulandshahr.
facts: Place: Khurja, Bulandshahr district
Typical look: hand-painted flowers, blue and earthy tones
GI: application 178, filed 2009, certificate dated 23 March 2015
Also an ODOP product of Bulandshahr
art: Khurja is known as the Ceramic City. Its pottery is glazed and hand-painted, often with floral patterns in greens, reds, blues and browns, with black used for borders (Incredible India). Homegrown says Mughal-era potters were known for underglaze floral and geometric designs, and that the blue shades were once a closely guarded secret.

Incredible India says the clay is a white clay (safed mitti) mixed with quartz and feldspar brought from Gujarat and Rajasthan. Homegrown gives the steps: raw materials are mixed with water and dried, softened clay is shaped in moulds, the shapes air-dry for a day or two, patterns are painted by hand, then glazed and fired in a kiln and cooled slowly to prevent cracking. Kilns have moved from coal to gas.
Today Khurja makes crockery, art wares, tiles and serveware. Homegrown says some producers make custom-glazed stoneware for restaurants in India and abroad.
artist: The potters are families who have worked in the trade for generations. Homegrown features Sayeed Ahamed, an artisan from a long line of potters. Many potters have called themselves Multani Kumhars, tracing roots to Multan, now in Pakistan.

Counts of the work force differ by source. Incredible India says about 25,000 workers plus 5,000 to 7,000 in support services, Homegrown says over 15,000, and Wikipedia cites about 500 units. All are estimates.
I could not find a reliable account of present-day wages or hardships, so none are stated here.
place: Khurja is a town in Bulandshahr district, western Uttar Pradesh, at about 28.25 N, 77.86 E. Wikipedia says it was founded in the 1400s by the Kheshgi family, a Pashtun ruling family.
Under the One District One Product scheme, ceramics is the product of Bulandshahr, and Khurja is the heart of that cluster.

Modern manufacturing grew in the 1940s. Wikipedia says the United Provinces government opened a pottery factory in 1942, which closed in 1946-47 over quality problems, and in 1952 the site became the Pottery Development Centre.

history.what: Sources place the start here. Some say Timur's army left potters behind, or brought potters from Egypt, Syria and elsewhere. Others say Mughal patrons were first. Homegrown notes the two versions conflict. The scholar Baidyanath Saraswati is quoted calling Khurja an old centre of glazed pottery.
Another account says potters were moved to the area in the 1500s under the Mughals (Wikipedia).
A government pottery factory opens in 1942, closes in 1946-47, and in 1952 becomes the Pottery Development Centre.
The GI application is filed on 6 July 2009. The registry gives the certificate date as 23 March 2015. Other pages give 2008 or 2008-09, which I could not match to the registry.
Kilns shift from coal to natural gas, and the ODOP scheme pushes exports (Homegrown).

future: Training: keep hand-painting and glazing skills alive with apprenticeships beside the factory work.
Livelihood: help small family units reach buyers as well as large factories, since ODOP gains may not always reach small artisans.
Materials: more clean-fuel kilns, and secure supplies of quartz and feldspar.
Documentation: record the traditional designs and the old blue glazes with the potter families.
Protection: use the 2015 GI to separate hand-made Khurja ware from imitations.

name: Kinhal Toys
tagline: Soft-wood gods, animals and palanquins, joined with tamarind-seed paste and painted by Chitragar families.
facts: Place: Kinhal (Kinnal), Koppal district
Makers: the Chitragar community
Wood: light woods such as white catamaran
GI tag 2012 per Incredible India
art: Kinhal toys, also called Kinnal craft, are small painted wooden figures. The Incredible India page lists idols of Hindu deities, palanquins, animals, models of fruit and vegetables, stools, masks and cradles. Their themes come mostly from Shaiva and Vaishnava stories.

The wood is light. Incredible India names white catamaran (polki), ivory wood and drumstick among the soft woods, and neem, mango and tamarind among the hard woods. Parts are carved separately and joined with a paste. The paste is made of crushed tamarind seeds, and sources differ slightly on the details.

A filler called kitta corrects shapes. Wikipedia describes it as powdered jute rags with sawdust and tamarind-seed paste. The South First article instead gives neem powder, tamarind seed powder and jute. A paste of powdered stone and gum (gachu) is used to raise jewellery and decoration. Cotton soaked in tamarind paste goes over the joins, and a pebble paste forms the base for paint.
The figures are hand-painted in bright colours and then varnished. South First says natural dyes are used along with a family-made colour called Lajjavar.
artist: The makers are the Chitragars, a community of painters and sculptors in the Koppal and Bellary region. Santosh Kumar Anjaneya Chitragar, a fine arts graduate from Kinnal, leads a team of ten artisans, according to the South First report.

That report says 67 families were traditionally involved in the craft and only 25 to 30 remain. Many former artisans now work as house painters or in garages. Orders for idols have fallen, and Santosh has changed colours and tones for buyers who were unsure about bringing religious idols into the home.

Wikipedia says the artisans believe their ancestors painted murals at the Pampapateshwara temple in Hampi and made wooden chariot work there. It marks the claim as needing a citation, and the page also mentions old paper tracings kept in one family home as support.
place: Kinhal is a village in Koppal taluk of Koppal district, on the west side of the Tungabhadra River according to Incredible India. Koppal town is the nearest large town.
The village lies close to Hampi, which fits the craft's traditional link with Vijayanagara. Sources also place Chitragar families in neighbouring Bellary district.

history.what: Incredible India says the toys are at least 500 years old and rooted in the Vijayanagara Empire, whose kings are said to have given Kinhal to the artisans as an inam (land grant).

After Vijayanagara fell, Incredible India says the Nawab of Koppal, the Desais of Kinhal and Nawab Salar Jung of Hyderabad supported the craft. The page prints the fall as 1665; the usual date is 1565.
South First says historians speculate that the artisans who carved Hampi's temples scattered, which weakened the craft.
Wikipedia says students from the University of Glasgow and the Glasgow School of Art worked with the Crafts Council of Karnataka on a revival project.
Kinhal Toys receive a GI tag, per Incredible India. One Wikipedia page gives GI number 159.
Only a few families remain, and young artisans such as Santosh Chitragar are adapting colours and products.

future: Training: set up apprenticeships in the remaining Chitragar families so that carving, kitta work and painting are passed on.
Livelihood: develop everyday products such as toys and home items, along with temple idols, so that income does not depend on two or three orders a year.
Materials: keep supplying light woods and tamarind seed, and record each natural colour recipe.
Documentation: record the surviving families and the old tracings kept in their homes.
Protection: use the GI tag to separate hand-made Kinhal pieces from factory copies.

name: Kolhapuri Chappals
tagline: Hand-stitched leather sandals, shaped over generations by Chambhar and Dhor families.
facts: Form: all-leather handmade sandal, traditionally of buffalo hide
GI granted 2018 to 2019 for eight districts in two states
Districts: Kolhapur, Sangli, Satara, Solapur, Belgaum, Dharwad, Bagalkot, Bijapur
A pair can take up to six weeks, Wikipedia reports
art: The Kolhapuri chappal is a flat, open leather sandal. The GI description, as discussed on SpicyIP, says it is all-leather and handmade, with the stitching and decoration also done in leather. Wikipedia adds that it is traditionally made from buffalo hide and thread, without nails.

An older, thinner form was called kanwali, from its two side flaps that looked like ears, according to Madras Courier. The same article says the footwear was known locally by another name before it was called Kolhapuri in the 18th century.

Making is a chain of hands. Madras Courier reports that the Mahar-Mang community collected hides, the Dhor caste tanned them and the Chambhar caste made the chappals. Wikipedia says a pair can take up to six weeks.
artist: The people behind the chappal are mostly from Scheduled Caste communities, as Madras Courier notes: Chambhar cobblers, Dhor tanners and Mahar-Mang hide collectors. Their work is skilled and has long been paid little.

The chain has been strained. SpicyIP explains that makers traditionally used hides of dead draught cattle, a supply that fell as tractors replaced bullocks, and that a 2015 amendment to the Maharashtra Animal Preservation Act made raw material harder to get. Madras Courier adds that hides now often come from Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and that many Kolhapur tanneries have closed.
Our approach: name the families and workshops, and show the whole chain from hide to heel.
place: Kolhapur, on the Panchganga river in southern Maharashtra, gives the sandal its name. The craft is not limited to the city. The GI covers eight districts: Kolhapur, Sangli, Satara and Solapur in Maharashtra, and Belgaum, Dharwad, Bagalkot and Bijapur in Karnataka.

That shared geography is why both states applied together. SpicyIP reports a joint application by the leather development corporations of Maharashtra and Karnataka (LIDCOM and LIDKAR). Madras Courier says many Karnataka artisans have long made these sandals, and that the footwear spread south to Telangana and Andhra Pradesh as well.

history.what: Madras Courier says the chappal began in 12th-century Kolhapur, with King Bijjala of Karnataka encouraging footwear making, though it did not take off until the 13th century. Wikipedia gives a much later start for the present design, so sources differ.
Wikipedia says Shahu of Kolhapur encouraged the trade and that 29 tanning centres opened in his time. Madras Courier says the Saudagar family later built a business supplying Mumbai stores.
Wikipedia credits the Saudagar family with starting and designing the modern form in this year.
SpicyIP reports a joint application for GI by the Maharashtra and Karnataka leather corporations.
The GI was registered in December 2018 according to SpicyIP, and reported in July 2019 by Wikipedia.
A Maharashtra ban on slaughter of cattle progeny tightened the hide supply, per SpicyIP and Madras Courier.

Wikipedia reports that Prada showed sandals resembling Kolhapuri chappals in a collection without naming their origin. After criticism it acknowledged the Indian inspiration, and a petition on artisan compensation was filed in the Bombay High Court.

future: Training: pay master cobblers to teach young people cutting, plaiting and stitching.
Livelihood: ensure the GI works for artisans, not only for brands. SpicyIP argues the tag alone does not guarantee income.
Materials: secure affordable, legal hides and support the remaining local tanneries.
Documentation: register authorised users and record designs, as the GI process allows.
Protection: set up a joint watchdog across the two states to act against copies, as SpicyIP suggests.

name: Kondapalli Toys
tagline: Light wood dolls of gods, farmers and village scenes, stuck together with tamarind-seed paste.
facts: Wood: tella poniki, a softwood from the Kondapalli hills
Joined with makku, a paste of tamarind seed powder and sawdust
Best known set: the Dasavatara
Geographical Indication registered in the mid-2000s
art: Kondapalli toys are carved from tella poniki, a light softwood that grows in the nearby Kondapalli hills. Each part of a figure is carved separately. The pieces are joined with makku, a paste of tamarind seed powder and sawdust, which also adds fine detail.
The toys are then coloured with oil or water colours, vegetable dyes or enamel paints, depending on the type. A Homegrown article says artisans use natural dyes as well as bright acrylics.
Subjects come from mythology and village life. The best known is the Dasavatara, the ten forms of Vishnu. Others show farmers, toddy tappers, marriage processions, animals, birds and bullock carts.
Toys are part of Bommala Koluvu, the festive display of dolls at Sankranti and Navaratri.
artist: The makers are called Aryakshatriyas, also written Nakarshalu. Wikipedia says they are mentioned in the Brahmanda Purana and are said to have come from Rajasthan in the 16th century. This is tradition, and I did not find independent proof.
Families work in the settlement known as Bommala Colony, and the skill passes down within families. Wikipedia says toys were traditionally put together at home around Sankranti and Navaratri.
I did not find individual artisans named in the sources I read.
place: Kondapalli is a village in Krishna district, a short way from Vijayawada. The hills around it give the wood the craft depends on.
Homegrown reports that shrinking forest resources threaten the supply of tella poniki. This is one of the main pressures on the craft.

history.what: Sources describe the craft as about 400 years old, and say the artisans worked under local royal patronage. Exact dates are not documented in what I read.
Tradition says the artisans migrated from Rajasthan.

SpicyIP reported in February 2007 that the GI Registry in Chennai had granted GI protection, calling it only the second handicraft from the state to receive it. Other sources give 2005 or 2006-07, so the exact year is uncertain.
Wikipedia says Andhra Pradesh's Republic Day parade float in 2025 was based on Kondapalli toys.

future: Secure legal access to tella poniki, and grow it in managed plantations, so the craft does not depend on a shrinking forest supply.
Train young family members and pay them well enough to stay, since sources say low profits and long hours push the young away.
Help artisans compete with plastic toys by selling the story and the maker's name.
Document the old figure sets, such as the Dasavatara and village sets, in photographs and measured drawings.
Use the GI to stop imitations, and make sure the benefit reaches artisan families.

name: Longpi Pottery
tagline: Black pottery shaped by hand, without a wheel.
facts: Medium: stone and clay mixture
Technique: hand-moulded, no potter's wheel
Finish: polished black
art: Longpi pottery is a dark, burnished pottery made from a local mix of stone and clay, without a wheel. Pots are shaped by hand, dried and fired.
Shapes include cooking pots, jars, cups and vases, and many are plain, with the beauty in the form and the shining surface.
artist: Longpi pottery is made by the Tangkhul Naga community, and especially by the women of Longpi villages, who learn it from their mothers and grandmothers.
Our approach: tell the story from stone gathering to firing.
place: Ukhrul district lies in the hills of eastern Manipur, home to the Tangkhul Nagas. Longpi Kajui is the village most associated with this craft.
The hills' land and festivals shape community life.

history.what: The craft is a long-standing community skill, used for cooking and storage.
Interest from craft markets has led to new decorative forms.

future: Tell the story of the community, not only the pot.
Train young potters and document the firing technique.
Improve road and market access from the hills.

name: Madur Mats
tagline: Cool floor mats woven from marsh sedge, from daily use to fine masland.
facts: Material: Cyperus pangorei, called madurkathi
Madurkathi GI registered 28 March 2018 (no. 567)
Three kinds: ekh-rokha, do-rokha, masland
Sharta village in Sabang block is the main hub
art: Madur mats are woven from madurkathi, a marsh sedge. Wikipedia says the mats are used for sitting and as bedding, and that they absorb sweat and do not conduct heat, so they suit the humid climate.

There are three kinds. Ekh-rokha is thin, with a single reed weft. Do-rokha has a double weft and is heavier. Masland is the finest and dearest, needs at least two weavers and is likened to sari weaving. Motifs include flowers, honeycomb and rhombus designs.

The reed's own colour does most of the work. Vegetable dyes give black from haritaki and babla bark, and reddish-maroon from annatto seeds. Village Square says a fine masland can sell for about Rs 1.5 lakh and weigh only 200 to 250 grams.
artist: Wikipedia says weavers are mainly Mahishya artisans, mostly women. Village Square describes about 4,500 artisans over six blocks.
Village Square names several: Alak Kumar Jana, an award-winning craftsman, Gouri Bala Das, Mithu Rani Jana, who visited Denmark in 2017, and Akhil Jana, who has promoted the craft abroad.
Weavers have diversified into table mats, bags, hats and spectacle cases as demand for floor mats has fallen.
place: The sedge grows in the alluvial soil of Medinipur, where flooding makes much land hard to farm. Reeds grow in two seasons, April to July and September to November.
Sharta village in Sabang block has over 450 families in the work. Wikipedia names Kasijora and Narajol as past centres.

history.what: Wikipedia connects mat weaving to the Indus Valley, a claim I treat as general.
Masland is said to have begun with silk-weft mats made in Medinipur.
Mats were collected as revenue, with Kasijora and Narajol key centres.
The census counted 618 mat-making workers in Medinipur.
Madurkathi receives a GI tag, applied for by the West Bengal Khadi and Village Industries Board.

future: Training: teach masland weaving to new weavers, which needs two skilled hands.
Livelihood: direct export links, since artisans say shipping is hard.
Materials: protect the marshes where the sedge grows.
Documentation: record weaver names and pattern names.
Protection: use the GI against imitations.

name: Majuli Masks
tagline: Masks of gods and demons, made by monks on a river island.
facts: Medium: bamboo, clay, cloth, cow dung
Use: Bhaona devotional theatre
Characters: Ravana, Garuda, Hanuman and others
art: The masks of Majuli are made for Bhaona, a form of religious theatre created by the saint Srimanta Sankardeva in the 15th–16th centuries. Actors wear them to become gods, demons, birds and beasts.
A mask is built on a bamboo frame, covered with clay and cloth, shaped and painted in natural colours. Some are small face masks, others cover the whole body.
artist: Majuli's satras, Vaishnava monasteries, are centres of art and learning, and monks make masks as a form of devotion. The Samaguri Satra is especially known for them.
Craft knowledge is handed from teacher to student within the monastery.
Our approach: let the satras guide what is shared and sold.
place: Majuli is a large river island in the Brahmaputra, in Assam, and has been called one of the world's largest river islands. It has long been a centre of Assamese Vaishnavite culture.
Flood and erosion have reduced the island over the decades.

history.what: Sankardeva and his disciples set up satras, with dance, drama and mask-making.
The satra tradition continued through the Ahom era.
Masks are made both for Bhaona and for sale to visitors.

future: Protect the island: link mask-making to river conservation and bank protection.
Keep the satras alive with young monks and students.
Record Bhaona performances alongside the masks.
