name: Meenakari
tagline: Glass colour fired onto gold and silver, with Jaipur's famous deep red.
facts: Form: enamel fused onto metal
Jaipur style: champlevé, known for deep red
Credited to Raja Man Singh of Amber bringing artisans from Lahore
Each colour is fired separately
art: Meenakari is the art of decorating metal with coloured enamel. Utsavpedia says the enamel is made from coloured glass powders and mineral oxides, and can be opaque, transparent or translucent. It is used on gold, silver and other metals, in designs of birds, flowers and leaves.

Itokri describes the steps. A design is made, the base is painted white or pink, and colours are applied in order of hardness. The piece is fired once for each colour. It is then cleaned and polished, and stones can be set in it.

Itokri says Jaipur developed champlevé enamelling, in which the design is cut into the metal and filled with colour, and that its deep red is the best known. The same page calls vivid red the hardest colour to get.
artist: Itokri calls the workers meenakars and says the skill passes down in families. The work is shared: a designer and goldsmith make the form, and the meenakar fills and fires the colour.
Itokri notes that enamel colours are brought from Amritsar, Germany and France, and that cheaper white metal is now used in place of gold, copper and silver in some work.
place: Jaipur is now the main centre, according to Utsavpedia. It says gold meenakari is mainly done in Jaipur, Banaras and Delhi, silver work in Udaipur, Bikaner and Nathdwara, and glass enamelling in Pratapgarh.
The craft grew with the court of Amber and Jaipur, whose rulers worked closely with the Mughals.

history.what: Utsavpedia says the craft began in Persia and came to India through the Mughals.

Both pages credit Raja Man Singh of Amber with bringing skilled artisans from Lahore to Rajasthan. Itokri puts this in the 16th century. The story is repeated widely, but I did not find an older source for it.
Itokri says close ties between the Mughal and Rajput courts led to a golden period for the craft.
Jaipur grew into the main centre and developed its own champlevé style, per Itokri.

future: Train young meenakars alongside goldsmiths and designers.
Support access to good enamel colours at fair prices.
Label hand-fired work clearly against base-metal imitations.
Document colour recipes and firing methods.
Link makers with designers and buyers who pay for slow work.

name: Mehndi
tagline: Henna paste drawn on skin, whose stain deepens over a day or two.
facts: Form: temporary skin decoration in henna paste
Plant: Lawsonia inermis, dried leaves ground to powder
Stain: starts orange, darkens over 24 to 72 hours
Word: from Sanskrit mendhika, the henna plant
art: Mehndi is the art of drawing on hands and feet with a paste made from the dried, powdered leaves of the henna plant. The paste is applied with a cone, brush or stick and left on for some hours. Wikipedia says it is then wrapped to hold warmth, and that the stain starts orange and darkens over one to three days. It fades in one to three weeks.

South Asian designs are described as small and fine, built from lines and patterns. Bridal work has become more elaborate in recent years, with fine lines, gilding and glitter, according to Wikipedia.

Mehndi goes with weddings, where an evening, often called Mehndi ki raat, is set aside for the bride, and sometimes the groom. It is also used at Karva Chauth, Diwali, Teej and Raksha Bandhan, and by Muslim families at Eid and Chaand Raat. In Kerala, brides and girls decorate their hands with mailanchi.

Black henna is a danger. Wikipedia warns that pastes sold as black henna may contain para-phenylenediamine (PPD), which can cause blistering, scarring and lifelong allergy. Pure henna is a brown to red stain.
artist: Mehndi is both a home art and a trade. Female relatives often apply it at weddings, and many professional mehndi artists now work at bridal events and shops.
I did not find a reliable source that names a particular master of mehndi, so I have named none.

The plant also has its own growers. Sojat, in Pali district of Rajasthan, is described by Wikipedia as a hub of henna cultivation, and it says Sojat mehndi has a GI certificate. That page gives no date for the registration, so please check the GI registry.
place: Mehndi is found across India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, and in the Middle East and North Africa. In India it follows the wedding season in every region.

Sojat, in Rajasthan, is the best-known place for growing and grinding the leaf. Wikipedia says the town's climate and soil suit the plant and calls it the only region in India where henna is grown for export. I could not confirm that claim from a second source. Pali and Jodhpur districts are nearby.
The pins mark Sojat and a few cities where bridal mehndi is a large trade. The city pins are examples, and I have no source ranking them.

history.what: Wikipedia says henna use can be traced back to ancient Babylon and Egypt, and that it was used in medicine in 6th-century Arabia.
Wikipedia reports henna in India by the 4th century CE from Deccan cave art, but marks the claim as weakly sourced. Treat it as unproven.
Henna probably became widespread in the subcontinent around now, which the article links to the rise of Islam here.
The Mughal empire is said to have made the custom more popular.
Mehndi nights, cones sold ready-made and fine bridal designs make it a large wedding trade.

future: Training: many artists learn by practice and from family. Short courses and online lessons are growing.
Livelihood: bridal mehndi artists earn from weddings and festivals, so their work is seasonal. Growers in Sojat depend on the leaf trade.
Materials: buyers should ask for pure henna and avoid black pastes with PPD. Sellers can label contents clearly.
Documentation: regional patterns and the local names for them are poorly recorded and could be collected with the women who draw them.
Protection: Sojat mehndi is said to hold a GI. The status should be checked against the GI registry.

name: Mizo Cane and Bamboo Craft
tagline: Baskets, hats, pipes and furniture from the bamboo that surrounds every Mizo village.
facts: Makers: men for cane and bamboo, women for weaving (IGNCA)
Items: baskets, lukhum hats, stools, traps, pipes
Craft centres: Aizawl, Lunglei, Chimtuipui (Saiha)
Technique: cane smoked to a mahogany-brown shine
art: IGNCA calls bamboo and cane crafts a major source of income for Mizoram. Baskets carry firewood, water, paddy, rice and vegetables, or store valuables. Named types include paikawng, emsin, paiem, tlamen, dawrawn, fawng and thul.

Hats include the lukhum, a peaked hat with two woven layers, and the japi rain hat. Furniture includes the herhsawp stool and thuttleng chair. There are also fish and crab traps, cages, umbrella handles, knitting needles and toys such as a bamboo pop-gun.
Smoking pipes are made: the men's bamboo pipe, the vaibel, and the women's clay-and-bamboo pipe, the tuibur.

Basketry uses plaited bamboo reinforced with stout cane. Cane is smoked for a shiny mahogany-brown colour and patterns. Stool rings are made by coiling fresh cane round a post and drying it in the sun. Some containers are made from whole culms with the nodes cleared out.
artist: IGNCA says women excel at weaving and men are expert at cane and bamboo work. Wikipedia says artisans work alone or in groups with simple tools.

Handicraft centres in Aizawl, Lunglei and Chimtuipui (Saiha) make traditional baskets and decorative articles. The Luangmual centre in Aizawl makes Mizo cane hats. I found no individual artisans named.
place: Mizoram's hills are rich in bamboo. IGNCA also notes that the Lushai build most of these items and that bamboo is plentiful but underused.
Bamboo is also used to build houses, with bamboo walls and matting floors, thatched roofs and cane-bound joints.

history.what: Wikipedia says Mizo craftsmanship dates back to ancient times, with cane and bamboo weaving at its core. No dated origin is given.
IGNCA describes bamboo used for houses, baskets, traps, pipes and toys as part of daily life.
A government factsheet reported in search results says bamboo furniture and bamboo or cane handicrafts fall under a 5 percent GST rate. I did not open this page.

future: Training: vocational training in cane and bamboo work, which IGNCA says authorities have considered.
Livelihood: expand markets beyond local use for hats, baskets and furniture.
Materials: make better use of the plentiful bamboo through treatment and design.
Documentation: record the Mizo names of baskets and their uses.
Protection: check for a Geographical Indication for signature items such as the lukhum.

name: Monpa Masks and Handmade Paper
tagline: Paper pounded from a shrub's bark for prayer wheels, and masks that bring monastery dances to life.
facts: Paper: Mon Shugu, from the inner bark of the Shugu Sheng shrub (Daphne papyracea)
Masks: used in cham, the monastic mask dance
Community: Monpa, Tawang
Paper-making village: Mukto, Tawang district
art: Mon Shugu is the handmade paper of the Monpa. It is made from the inner bark of a shrub the Monpa call Shugu Sheng, or paper plant. The bark is dried, boiled with an ash solution, beaten to pulp and cut into sheets by hand. Sources say no chemical additives are used.

Monks have used the paper to write Buddhist scriptures, mantras and sutras, and for the texts placed inside prayer wheels. Today it is also made into handbags, envelopes and bases for paintings. One report says it is stronger than ordinary paper; that figure comes from a single quoted local advocate, so treat it as his claim.

Monpa masks are three-dimensional sculpted forms of gods and spirits from Buddhism. Humans of North East writes that they are used only in performances or on special occasions and trace back to Tibetan culture. Another source says the Monpa also make masks showing animals such as the yak.

The masks belong to cham, a ritual mask dance in monasteries. Sahapedia describes it as a sacred practice performed by monks and nuns, in which wrathful deities and protectors are invoked to drive away evil spirits. In Tawang and West Kameng the Monpa perform it at the Torgya festival before Losar. Masks include deer, Garuda, crocodile, lion and skeleton forms.
artist: Paper-making was traditionally done by a handful of families in Mukto village. Down To Earth-linked reporting says six to seven families once did it. A 2022 PTI report says only four or five households do it now. Skills pass down in families.

The 2022 report names Sangey Dorjee, 57, who has made paper since age seven, and Thinley Gombo, 53, who hopes one of his children will return to the craft. Nima Tsering, 24, wants to sell the paper on social media. The makers formed the Traditional Paper and Handicraft Marketing Society.

Maling Gombu, a Tawang social worker and lawyer, wrote to the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) in February 2020 about reviving the craft. I could not find named mask-makers in the sources I could read.
place: Tawang is a high-altitude district in western Arunachal Pradesh, near the Bhutan and Tibet borders, and the home of the Monpa. Its main monastery, Gaden Namgyal Lhatse, is noted by Sahapedia as a place where cham is performed.

Mukto village in Tawang district is where the paper tradition survives. Sources say the shrub is scattered and hard to gather at high altitude, and courier service exists only at the district headquarters, which raises delivery costs.

history.when: Traditionally said to be about 1,000 years
history.what: Reports on the paper call it about a thousand years old. I found no archival evidence for the date, so read it as a local and press claim.
One article says Monpa paper was once sold to Tibet, Bhutan, Thailand and Japan, and that the trade declined as cheaper Chinese paper arrived.
Sahapedia credits Padmasambhava with starting monastic cham about 1,300 years ago in Tibetan monasteries. Dates here are traditional, not firm.
UNDP and KVIC set up machinery at a common facility in Mukto. It did not take off and the equipment was later moved to Tawang.
Maling Gombu wrote to KVIC about reviving the paper.
A KVIC-run unit opened in Tawang. The Better India reports about 500 to 600 sheets a day and Rs 400 daily earnings for artisans.
Makers in Mukto formed a marketing society and planned to sell online.

future: Training: teach younger Monpa the paper and mask crafts, as the KVIC unit has begun to do with local women and men.
Livelihood: sell through online marketplaces and shops, and find ways to cut courier costs from Mukto.
Materials: work with the forest department on a Shugu Sheng plantation, since the shrub takes years to regrow and is scattered.
Documentation: record mask forms and their meanings with monasteries, and the paper-making steps with senior makers.
Protection: check the official GI registry for the paper's status; sources I read disagree and I could not confirm it.

pins.label: Tawang (Gaden Namgyal Lhatse Monastery area, approx.)

name: Moradabad Brassware
tagline: The Brass City, where lamps and bowls are poured from molten metal into river sand.
facts: Nickname: Peetal Nagri, the Brass City
Core method: sand casting of brass
GI: 'Moradabad Metal Craft' (sources give 2013 or 2014)
Also part of Uttar Pradesh's One District One Product scheme
art: Moradabad is known as Peetal Nagri, the Brass City. Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, prized for being hard and easy to work. Moradabad's products include lamps, prayer bowls, bells and idols.

A People's Archive of Rural India (PARI) report from 2024 describes casting in detail. Brass ingots are melted in a coal-fired furnace. Sand is packed into a mould container around a shaped form to leave a hollow. Molten brass is poured in, and the cast piece is taken out and trimmed. Extra brass is broken off and melted again, and the sand is reused.
The PARI article lists common cast products as prayer bowls (chandan piyali), lamps (diya) and Om symbols, many supplied to temples across India.

After casting, pieces pass to other workers for surface work. PARI mentions the colouring of metal surfaces, called meena work, and packing. Drishti IAS notes that electroplating, lacquering and powder coating came into the craft in the 1980s.
artist: PARI speaks with casters in the city. Mohammad Aslam, 55, has cast for about 40 years and says his daily earnings are about Rs 500, against Rs 250 ten years earlier. Raees Jaan, 60, runs the furnace and began work at ten. Mohammad Subhan, 24, also works as an electrician in the wedding season.

PARI reports that casters work around 12 hours a day in cramped, hot spaces. Aslam estimates that about 90 per cent of the workforce is Muslim. Casters told the reporters that their situation had not improved since the GI tag.
Hard work and low pay have turned younger men to other tasks such as colouring, packing and boxing, PARI says.
place: Moradabad lies in western Uttar Pradesh, on the Ramganga river, at about 28.83 N, 78.78 E. Wikipedia says it was founded in 1624 by the Mughal governor Rustam Khan Dakhani, who refounded the town of Chaupala, and that under Shah Jahan it was renamed for Prince Murad Bakhsh. Another source gives a different founding story, so treat the details as uncertain.

Wikipedia reports that metalcraft exports from Moradabad reach more than 80 countries. Estimates of jobs vary widely, from about 150,000 to 800,000, and most of the industry is unorganised. In 2018, about 75 units were shut over pollution of the Ramganga, and makers have since diversified into iron, steel and aluminium.
Drishti IAS reports that the city's brassware sells in the US, Britain, Canada, Germany and the Middle East, and that demand for idols rose with the building of the Ram temple at Ayodhya.

history.what: Moradabad is founded (Wikipedia gives 1624 in its history section and 1625 in its infobox). It is later renamed after Prince Murad Bakhsh.
Popular sources link the brass trade to Mughal-era demand and to later British-era exports. I did not find a primary source that fixes dates, so these are traditional accounts.
The industry widens from brass into iron and aluminium wares, with electroplating, lacquering and powder coating, according to Drishti IAS.
'Moradabad Metal Craft' is registered as a Geographical Indication. PARI says 2014; other pages say 2013.
About 75 units are shut over pollution of the Ramganga river (Wikipedia).

Exports fall during and after the Covid-19 pandemic, from about Rs 10,000 crore in 2018-19 to an estimated Rs 6,500 crore in 2021-22 (Wikipedia). PARI's caster Mohammad Subhan says he lost his savings in the lockdown.
Demand for temple idols revives some orders, according to Drishti IAS.

future: Training: casting is the hardest and worst-paid step, so pay it better and teach young workers the furnace and mould skills.
Livelihood: raise caster wages, which PARI says have barely moved, and link small workshops directly to buyers.
Materials: cleaner fuel and furnaces, since coal costs and Ramganga pollution both hit the trade.
Documentation: record the many hands of the craft, from casters to finishers, with their own names.
Protection: use the GI so that Moradabad work can be told from imitations, and make sure its benefits reach casters.

name: Naga Beadwork
tagline: Glass, carnelian and chank shell strung into necklaces that showed rank at festivals.
facts: Both men and women wear beaded ornaments
Angami of Khonoma made chank shell beads and traded them
Carnelian and glass beads came through trade from India and beyond
Traditional jewellery making had largely stopped by the 1970s, per a dealer's essay
art: Naga necklaces combine glass beads, carnelian and shell. A dealer's essay on an Angami necklace describes ten strands of glass trade beads, long chank shell beads, shell plaques and bone spacers. Clear orange carnelian beads from Gujarat are described as likely 18th century.
The IGNCA craft page says glass beads, including trade beads, are strung on local fibre cords and fastened with coins. It also says broken thick glass tumblers were turned into ear ornaments.

Chank shell (Turbinella pyrum) comes from the Indian Ocean. The Angami of Khonoma made beads from the central column of the shell and traded them to other Naga groups, according to the same essay. Shell pendants hang down the back as a counterweight, so only the beaded strand shows at the front.
artist: The dealer's essay says these necklaces were prestige pieces for important festivals, and the most elaborate were worn by warriors. Rank was earned, so jewellery offered a path up in standing. Jewellery was thought to have a spirit.

Jewellery was treated as heirloom property, and beads were reused and remade as a family grew richer. Some groups made no ornaments and bought them from others. Naga buyers were choosy and refused poor beads, the essay says, citing Untracht (1997).
I found no named living bead artists in the sources I read.
place: Khonoma is an Angami village in Kohima district and is named in sources as the source of shell beads. The shells themselves came from the Bay of Bengal region and beads from India and as far as Venice.
The Naga live mainly in eastern India, with some in western Burma. The essay counts at least 15 subgroups.

history.what: Early Gujarati carnelian beads in some necklaces are dated to the 18th century by one dealer, who gives no proof I could check.
The dealer dates the Angami necklace described here to this period.
Beads and shells arrive through trade from India, the Bay of Bengal and Europe.
The essay says traditional jewellery making had largely stopped, and heirlooms were sometimes sold for medicine or household goods.
Nagaland becomes a state, per the same essay.

future: Training: bead stringing and shell cutting are skills that could be taught by elders in Khonoma and other villages.
Livelihood: new jewellery for local and online buyers can sit beside heirloom repair.
Materials: glass beads are now bought, and real chank shell is costly. Honest labels for materials help buyers.
Documentation: museums and private collections hold many pieces. Records in the community, of which tribe wore what, would help.
Protection: heirlooms leave the state through sales, and families need support to keep them.

name: Naga Pottery
tagline: Hand-built pots, made by women without a wheel and fired on bamboo.
facts: Women's craft; no potter's wheel is used
Changki (Ao) potters: about 15 women still make pots at home
Pots are fired outdoors with bamboo
Khuzama, an Angami pottery village, no longer practises the craft
art: Pottery is not widely practised in Nagaland. The IGNCA page says it is restricted to women and made by hand without a revolving wheel, with methods that vary by tribe and area. Designs are often inspired by textile patterns.

At Changki in Mokokchung district, Ao women hand-build the pots. Rural India Online says clay is gathered from fields, hills, forests and riverbanks, and only clay from that altitude suits the pots. The pottery season runs from December to March, and a batch can take a month or more from shaping to firing. Bamboo is used to fire the pots outdoors. Tools such as the potsuro and nangbenba are made of local clay and wood.

At Khar village, also in Mokokchung district, potters soak and grind the clay by hand, shape it, dry the pots near a fireplace and burn them for several hours until reddish, using dried bamboo, according to Eastern Mirror.
The IGNCA page adds that a new pot is heated with paddy husks and boiled with rice water to remove the taste of fresh clay and make it last.
artist: Tiamongla Longchari, 55, a veteran potter of Changki, learned from her grandmother. She makes about 150 to 200 pots a year, depending on demand, health and farm work. Anokwala Lusang works at the Village Development Board women's studio, and Jentikala Amri returned to pottery after training started there.
Rural India Online says pots sell for Rs 600 to 900 and demand is usually higher than the potters can meet. Few young women take up the work because it is heavy and takes much time beside farming.
Eastern Mirror profiles two widows at Khar who make about 100 pots a month and sell them for Rs 100 to 350, with transport making marketing hard.
place: Changki lies in Mokokchung district, in the Ao area. The article says the Ao speak three languages, Chungli, Mongsen and Changki. The village studio was built with Village Development Board funds, and sales go to the board's corpus fund.

Khar is about 34 km from Mokokchung town, and its potters supply villages in Mokokchung and Wokha. Khuzama is a southern Angami village once famous for large quantities of fine pots. A journal article says the craft is no longer practised there.

history.what: Rural India Online says Changki pots once served in local wars and for cooking, and grain was sent in them as food aid after village fires.
Pots were once made in nearly every Changki household. Now only 15 women make them at home.
The Angami village was known for its pots, but the craft has faded, and the author says hands-on learning from a skilled potter is needed.
The village board built a studio and a four-room market on the highway from pottery funds.
Longpi black stone pottery is a separate Tangkhul tradition from Ukhrul, Manipur, so I do not count it here. I found no source for pottery at Chumukedima.

future: Training: Changki's studio lets younger women learn beside veterans. Paid apprenticeships would encourage more to join.
Livelihood: demand exceeds supply, so better prices and steady bulk orders could keep potters earning.
Materials: good clay is gathered from distant sites. Clay beds and bamboo fuel need to be kept accessible.
Documentation: Khuzama shows how quickly skills go. Filming and written records, along with teaching, are needed.
Protection: a Changki mark or GI listing could help, but I found no existing status.

name: Nettipattam
tagline: The golden forehead cover that makes a temple elephant shine at the Pooram.
facts: Meaning: netti (forehead) + pattam (band)
Medium: gilded copper plates and bubbles on red velvet
Use: temple festivals, especially Thrissur Pooram
Types: chooralpoli, nagapadam, vandodu
art: The nettipattam is the golden caparison worn on the forehead of a temple elephant in Kerala. It is only one part of the full set of elephant finery, which also has fly-whisks of yak hair (venchamaram), peacock-feather fans (alavattom), silk parasols (muthukuda), bells and neck ropes.

It is made of hemispherical plates and small bubbles, called kinnam or kumila, of copper, sometimes brass, painted or coated with gold, stitched on red velvet with woollen borders and tied with a cotton rope. A published count lists about 5,000 small bubbles on one piece, plus larger half-moon plates and a pointed central piece.

There are several patterns. Chooralpoli is described as the finest and is for the main elephant; nagapadam, with serpent-head plates, is for the second and third elephants; vandodu has shell-like plates and is the base form.

Some writers give the bubbles a symbolic meaning, such as the five elements and nine planets. A Sahapedia essay says the pattern was devised by Kirangattu Namboothiri and first used at the Peruvanam Pooram, but this is described as a belief, not a record.
artist: The sources we read describe the work but name no single maker or workshop, so we do not name them. A news report says one temple devaswom engaged about 25 artists in its camp to prepare the ornaments for a Pooram.
Caparisons are mostly made in Thrissur, with Thrippunithura named as another centre. The work combines metalworkers, who shape the plates, and tailors and decorators, who sew and arrange them.
Commercial listings in the Thrissur area also offer cheaper polymer and plastic replicas.
Our approach: visit the workshops during the months before the Pooram and let the makers tell us their names and families.
place: Thrissur is called the cultural capital of Kerala. The Vadakkunnathan temple stands on a hill in the middle of the town, with the open Thekkinkadu Maidan around it.

Thrissur Pooram, held in the month of Medam on the Pooram star, was started by Sakthan Thampuran, ruler of Kochi, in 1796, according to Wikipedia. Two sides, Thiruvambady and Paramekkavu, face each other. In the Kudamattam, caparisoned elephants line up and silk umbrellas are changed rapidly.
Festival elephants and their finery need space, money and months of preparation, which is why Thrissur is the main centre. Caparisons and umbrellas are prepared fresh each year.
Elephant welfare rules are debated in Kerala and can affect how many elephants take part; we have not checked the current rules.

history.what: Brass, copper and gold ornaments for temple elephants are part of Kerala temple custom; a legend credits Brahma with the first forehead cover for Indra's elephant. This is myth, not date.
The Peruvanam Pooram is said to be where the nettipattam was first used, per one tradition.
Sakthan Thampuran starts Thrissur Pooram after temples are barred from the Arattupuzha Pooram.
Pooram grows into a great public festival; the finery is produced in large numbers.
Rules on elephants, cost and synthetic copies change the trade.

future: Document makers and families, and show their work at a small museum near the Vadakkunnathan temple.
Train a new set of metalworkers and decorators through apprenticeships.
Keep real metal pieces for the main occasions and label synthetic ones honestly.
Follow humane rules for the elephants: weight limits, rest and shade.
Open a pre-Pooram workshop trail so visitors see the work, not only the parade.
Support safe, lighter materials developed with makers so the art stays affordable.

name: Pattamadai Mats
tagline: Mats woven from river grass so fine that the best are called silk.
facts: Woven from korai grass in Tirunelveli district
Fine mats and superfine pattu pai
Made mostly by women weavers at Pathamadai
Has Geographical Indication status
art: The Pattamadai mat, also spelt Pathamadai pai, is woven from korai, a grass-like plant. The stalks are split into fine strands, and coloured, then woven on a floor loom with a cotton warp.

The weaver uses a long wooden needle called the kuchaali and a wooden tool, the achu, to press the weave tight. The News Minute describes two main types. Fine mats use commercially grown korai, with about 50 threads per 9 inches. Superfine mats, called pattu pai or silk mat, use wild korai from the Thamirabarani river area, with 100 to 140 threads per 9 inches.
Patterns are made by lifting the cotton warp threads, which asks for sharp eyesight. Drishti IAS notes mats made for weddings can carry the names of the bride and groom and the date woven into them.
artist: The News Minute reports that about 100 women in Pathamadai make the mats, mostly from the Muslim community. The craft has passed through at least five generations. S. Zeenath Beevi leads a self-help group of about 20 weavers, several of whom are state or district award winners.
Most weavers are related by birth or marriage. Men did much of the weaving 30 to 40 years ago, but many left for better pay. Women now weave from home, which lets them manage family work.
The report says weavers earn about Rs 9 an hour on average, though mats sell for Rs 1,500 to Rs 5,500 depending on size and thread count.
place: Pathamadai is a village in Tirunelveli district in the south of Tamil Nadu, on the plains near the Thamirabarani river. The river supplies the wild korai used for the finest mats.
The weavers work in homes and a shared workshop. The News Minute says the workshop stands on rented land and that the women hope to build their own.

history.what: Weavers say the craft has passed down at least five generations in Pathamadai.
Sources give 2012-13 or 2013 for the Geographical Indication registration, so the year is not settled.
Cheaper plastic mats, mechanised production and some use of synthetic dyes have put pressure on handmade work, according to Drishti IAS.

future: Raise weavers' pay through fair pricing and direct marketing.
Help the group buy or secure land for its own workshop.
Protect the wild korai along the river and its supply.
Train younger women and men in fine weaving and pattern work.
Use the GI to tell buyers how to spot a genuine handwoven mat.

name: Pietra Dura (Parchin Kari)
tagline: Coloured stones set into white marble so closely that the join disappears.
facts: Technique: stone pieces set in carved grooves in marble
Stones: lapis lazuli, turquoise, malachite, onyx, carnelian, jasper
Peak monument: the Taj Mahal, begun in the 1630s
Now centred on Agra and Fatehpur Sikri
art: In India the craft is called parchin kari, also pachchikari. Wikipedia translates it as inlay or driven-in work. In Europe the same family of work is called pietra dura, hard stone, and began in Florence. Wikipedia says the technique reached the Mughal court in the early 17th century and was adapted into a local style.

The Outlook article describes the process. Stones are cut and shaped on a hand-operated machine. The marble is carved with a chisel to make recesses. The stones are set piece by piece with an adhesive and then buffed and polished. A single flower may combine many tiny pieces.

Core77 describes how the work is done in Agra today. The marble is coated with henna paint, the outlines are scratched, and the grooves are cut. The stone is shaped on a human-powered grindstone. Each piece is ground one by one so that it fits with no gap. The glue is a paste of sugar cane, beeswax, honey, lemon juice, marble dust and lentils, the article says. The surface is finished with wax.
Stone colours were often chosen with meaning in mind. Live History India names lapis lazuli, carnelian and jade among the stones used.
artist: Core77 says the skill was passed only to men within the artisan families, and the author met descendants after about 14 generations. The artisans there work as a cooperative, each keeping creative freedom and sharing profits equally. Whether this holds for all workshops is not known.
Work is slow. The same article says labour-intensive pieces take several weeks, and finger tips are worn by the grindstone. Outlook says several artisans may work for days on one piece.

Today the craft mostly makes household items such as table tops, coasters, chess boards and cabinets, Outlook says. Live History India warns that few families still practise it. I did not find a reliable count of artisans.
place: Parchin kari is best known from Agra, where the Taj Mahal, the tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula and Agra Fort carry inlay. Outlook says the craft continues in the lanes of Agra and Fatehpur Sikri. The Taj Mahal uses translucent marble from Makrana in Rajasthan, according to Core77.

Agra's craftspeople are often described as descendants of the workers who built the Taj. This is the common local belief, and sources differ on the lineage. After the British took Agra, visitors wanted inlaid souvenirs, and this helped create a local industry.

The listing of Delhi in the state line reflects the Mughal capital. Sources I read speak only of Agra and Fatehpur Sikri for the present craft, so the Delhi pin marks the court city of the Mughals and not a living workshop cluster.

history.what: Live History India traces inlay back to Roman opus sectile and to Renaissance Italy, where it became pietra dura.
Live History India names the Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque in Delhi as an early Mughal example of inlay.
The tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula in Agra is built, an important step towards the full style.
Construction of the Taj Mahal begins. Sources give 1632 or 1633. Shah Jahan is said to have brought experts from Persia.
Mughal patronage fades, and artisans turn to decorative goods.
Visitors to Agra under British rule create demand for inlaid souvenirs.
The craft continues in Agra and Fatehpur Sikri on a smaller scale.

future: Training: the family system is shrinking, so open workshops where young people can learn grinding, cutting and fitting would help.
Livelihood: direct sale through craft platforms and fair-trade shops, with the maker named.
Materials: honest labelling of real and imitation stones so that buyers can tell the difference.
Documentation: record the process from henna marking to wax finish, and the family lines, in the artisans' own words.
Protection: care for the monuments themselves, where the old inlay is the best teaching piece.

name: Punjabi Jutti
tagline: A slip-on leather shoe, stitched about 400 times a pair, often with gold-coloured thread.
facts: Slip-on leather shoe with no left or right
Known as khussa in Pakistan and mojari in other parts of India
Tilla (metallic thread) embroidery on festive pairs
Made by Ramdasi Chamar and other leatherworking families
art: The jutti is a flat slip-on leather shoe that rises at the back, with a rounded or pointed toe. Wikipedia says it has no left or right and slowly takes the shape of the foot. The same style is called mojari elsewhere in India and khussa in Pakistan.

The Rural India report describes one hand-made pair: the upper is cowhide, the sole is buffalo hide, and the maker stitches with coarse cotton thread, piercing the leather about 400 times a pair. A deer horn is used to shape the toe from inside.

Embroidery is added with zari or tilla thread. In Fazilka, Sahapedia says women hand-embroider with an aari hook, and the work is dense. In Patiala, uppers are mostly machine-embroidered and the work is split among many homes.
Prices vary a lot. Sahapedia gives roughly Rs 2,000 to 5,000 for Fazilka pairs, worn at weddings and ceremonies, and Rs 400 to 1,500 for Patiala's everyday pairs.
artist: Leatherwork has traditionally been done by Dalit communities. The Rural India report names the maker Hans Raj of Rupana village, Muktsar, a Ramdasi Chamar who has made juttis for nearly 50 years. His wife Veerpal Kaur does the zari embroidery.

He earns about Rs 10,000 a month. His sons have not learned the craft, and he describes high leather prices and young people leaving the trade. The report notes he suffered a partial stroke in November 2023.
Sahapedia says in Fazilka men cut and build the shoe while women embroider, and in Patiala families specialise in single steps and are paid per piece.
place: Muktsar, Fazilka, Patiala and Amritsar are named as centres. Sahapedia says Patiala's makers trace their roots to Rajasthan, and that the Fazilka work is done in family homes near the border.
Tanned leather often comes from Jalandhar, far from Muktsar, which adds cost (Rural India). Juttis are exported to the Punjabi diaspora (Wikipedia).

history.what: Wikipedia mentions a wooden sandal of about 200 BC as 'believed' to be among the earliest, which is not specific to the jutti.
Some pages say the embroidered style is over 400 years old and royal in origin. Wikipedia marks this as lacking a source, so treat it as unconfirmed.
Sahapedia says the Patiala makers' ancestors came from Rajasthan under royal patronage and later settled in Punjab.
Rural India reports demand has revived over the past 10 to 15 years, while materials such as rexine are increasingly used.
The craft is split between slow hand work and cheaper, machine-assisted production.

future: Pay hand-stitchers fairly and label hand-made pairs honestly.
Teach young people the craft, and give them a share in design and sales.
Tackle the stigma attached to leather work and the closure of local tanneries.
Support access to good leather without long trips.
Document the methods of Fazilka and Muktsar before the older makers retire.

name: Ringal Bamboo Craft
tagline: Baskets, mats and cradles woven from the slender hill bamboo of the high Himalaya.
facts: Material: ringal, a dwarf hill bamboo
Products: baskets, mats, winnowing trays, cradles
Reported to have a GI tag (Oaklores)
More than 10,000 artisans, per a Video Volunteers report
art: Ringal is a slender hill bamboo that grows in large amounts at higher altitudes in Uttarakhand. Oaklores names the species Chimonobambusa falcata. Sources differ on the botanical name.
Farmers harvest the canes and split them into thin strips. The strips are soaked in water to soften them and then woven by hand with simple tools.

Traditional pieces include tokri (grain baskets), doka (large carrying baskets), suppa (winnowing trays), puthuka (grain containers) and jhoola (cradles). Video Volunteers adds that women carry firewood, manure and vegetables in ringal baskets, and that ringal shrines and umbrellas are carried to temples at festivals.
Artisans also make light furniture and decorative pieces, often with grass and other bamboo.
artist: Skills pass through families, and each maker adds a personal touch to traditional methods. Video Volunteers says harvesters and weavers in Garhwal's hill communities do this work, and that more than 10,000 artisans in the state make bamboo and ringal goods.
Luxmi Nautiyal, quoted in that report, says a ringal basket costs about Rs 50 and lasts six to seven years, and she hopes artisans are not replaced by a culture of plastic.
I could not open the pages on artisan groups such as the Alaknanda Ghaati Shilpi Federation, so I do not describe them.
place: The craft belongs to the hills of Garhwal and Kumaon, where ringal grows wild in the high forest. Chamoli is a centre.
The Forest Research Institute at Dehradun ran a five-day ringal training in March 2023 for 28 artisans from Ummedpur and Premnagar near Dehradun, covering seasoning and preservation.

history.what: No source I read gives a date for when ringal weaving began. It is described as an age-old household craft.
Cheap plastic goods took market share from ringal baskets, according to Oaklores and Video Volunteers.
Oaklores says ringal has received a GI tag. I could not open the registry page, so the year is not given here.
FRI Dehradun held a ringal handicraft training under its AICRP bamboo project.

future: Training: courses on seasoning, preserving and new designs, as FRI has begun, held in the hill villages.
Livelihood: link makers to buyers so that baskets sell for what the work is worth, and develop products beyond farm baskets.
Materials: harvest canes at the right time, sustainably, and share the rights to gather them fairly.
Documentation: record local names of baskets and weaves, and the makers.
Protection: use the GI to protect the name and tell buyers who the makers are.

name: Sarthebari Bell Metal
tagline: Hammered, golden-brown bell metal: the xorai that welcomes every guest in Assam.
facts: Alloy of about 78 parts copper to 22 parts tin
Best known product: the xorai, an offering tray on a stand
GI tag in 2024
Described as Assam's second largest handicraft after bamboo
art: Bell metal is an alloy of bronze with a high tin content. Wikipedia's article on the craft puts the mix at about 78 percent copper and 22 percent tin. In Sarthebari it is called kaah. It is melted in charcoal-fired furnaces and cast in hand-made clay moulds, then hammered into shape with hammers, chisels and anvils. Polishing with charcoal, clay and fibres gives the golden-brown sheen, and designs are engraved by hand.

The best known piece is the xorai, an offering tray on a stand, with or without a cover. Outlook Traveller says it holds tamul (areca nut) and paan offered to guests as a sign of welcome, and it is also used for prasad and as a gift. The same article lists botas (trays), bowls, plates and glasses found in many Assamese homes. Other pieces named are water pots, temple bells and cymbals.
Most of the work is by hand. Sarthebari is described as the hub of Assam's brass and bell metal industry, and the craft is called the second largest handicraft of Assam after bamboo.
artist: Wikipedia's craft article names the Kahar (also called Oja) communities as the traditional practitioners, with skills passed down within families. It also cites a Buranji passage saying the Ahoms obtained bell-metal workers, called kahar, after conquering the Chutia kingdom. That page carries a notice that parts of it may need checking, so treat the detail with care.
Work is shared between casters, beaters and finishers. No source we read gives an exact count of artisans. Reports vary, so we do not give a number.
Outlook Traveller reports that raw materials must be brought from other states and that rising costs make it hard for artisans to keep going.
place: Sarthebari is a town in Barpeta district, in the lower Brahmaputra valley, at about 26.35 N, 91.22 E. Wikipedia notes it was declared a town in 1955. It lies about 42 km from Barpeta Road railway station and about 71 km from Guwahati airport, according to Outlook Traveller.
Artisans in Hajo, nearer Guwahati, also make bell metal and brass items, and have adapted designs to modern tastes.

history.what: Wikipedia's craft article claims bell metal objects from Assam were exchanged as gifts in the time of King Bhaskar Varman. Treat this as a claim that needs checking.
Royal patronage is said to have supported the craft, and Sarthebari became the main production centre.
Sarthebari is declared a town.
The Government of India grants the Sarthebari Metal Craft a Geographical Indication tag; the Chief Minister announced it on 31 March 2024.

future: Livelihood: lower the cost of copper and tin through bulk buying or a raw-material depot for artisans.
Protection: use the GI tag against machine-made copies sold as Sarthebari work.
Training: pass casting and beating skills to younger family members and new learners.
Design: keep the xorai and temple pieces, and add new useful products with the artisans' own design input.
Documentation: record each stage and the tools by name, in Assamese, with the workers who use them.

name: Sawantwadi Lacquerware and Toys
tagline: Coral-wood toys, fruit baskets and hand-painted ganjifa cards from a Konkan palace town.
facts: Form: lacquered wooden toys, lacquerware and circular ganjifa cards
Wood: Indian coral tree (Erythrina variegata), called pangara in Marathi
Lacquerware reached Sawantwadi around the late 17th century
Main craft area: Chitarali market
art: Sawantwadi is known for lacquered wooden toys and for ganjifa, circular hand-painted playing cards. The toys are carved from the Indian coral tree, called pangara in Marathi, according to The Better India, and finished with a glossy lacquer, says Outlook Traveller.

The toys are things of daily life. Fruit and vegetable models are the best known: one artisan in The Better India makes a basket of 27 fruits. Outlook Traveller lists Bhatukli kitchen sets, soldiers modelled on Maratha regiments, animals and sets of deities for festivals.

Ganjifa cards are circular and hand painted in red, green, yellow and black. Outlook Traveller says the format has roots in Persia but that Sawantwadi's designs turned to Indian themes such as the Dashavatara, and that full 120-card Dashavatara sets are still painted by hand.
artist: The craft is linked to the Chitari community, whose name means painters. The Better India profiles Subhash Balkrishna Chitari, who has made toys for 62 years since the age of nine and is the fifth generation in his family in the trade. His son is following him.

He estimates that fewer than ten artisans in Sawantwadi still practise the craft. He names cheap imported toys, fake products sold as Sawantwadi toys, short delivery times and the cost of wood as reasons. Wood is scarcer because people once planted coral trees along field borders for toymakers and now cut them down.
Our approach: name the artisan families and show how a single fruit goes from a block of wood to a painted toy.
place: Sawantwadi is in Sindhudurg district, in the Konkan region on Maharashtra's west coast. Wikipedia places the town at about 16 degrees north, 73.75 east. It was the capital of the Sawant Bhonsle dynasty.

Wikipedia says lacquerware was brought around the end of the 17th century by Brahmins from Telangana and Andhra, who also brought ganjifa. Outlook Traveller says the craft area today is Chitarali market, and that part of the Sawantwadi palace has workshops where visitors can watch toy-making, chess-set carving and ganjifa painting.

history.what: Lacquerware and ganjifa arrive in Sawantwadi with Brahmin families from Andhra and Telangana, per Wikipedia and Outlook Traveller.
Wikipedia says schools of the craft developed.
Wikipedia says Khem Sawant II moved the capital to Sundarwadi, which became known as Sawantwadi. The article gives no firm date.
The Sawantwadi palace is built, in Konkan timber style with some Portuguese and British influence, says Outlook Traveller.
Wikipedia reports that a museum opened in the Sawantwadi palace.

Sources disagree on when the toys received a GI tag: dates from 2017 to 2024 appear in different reports, and Wikipedia says only that registration was being sought. We could not confirm the date in the GI registry.

future: Training: support young Chitari family members and others to learn carving and painting in structured apprenticeships.
Livelihood: fair prices and bulk orders from schools, museums and shops, with realistic delivery times.
Materials: plant coral trees again on farm borders so wood is available at a fair price.
Documentation: record the traditional toy and ganjifa designs and the artisans' families.
Protection: confirm the GI status and take action against fake products labelled as Sawantwadi.

name: Shola Pith Craft
tagline: A plant lighter than cork, carved into bridal crowns and the white glow of Durga's festival.
facts: Material: stem of Aeschynomene aspera, a marsh plant
Makers are traditionally the Malakar community
Used for wedding headgear (topor) and idol decoration
Estimates of artisans vary; one source says about 5,000
art: Shola, also called sholapith or Indian cork, is a dried, milky-white, spongy plant material. It comes from Aeschynomene aspera, a herb that grows wild in marshy, waterlogged land in Bengal, Assam and Odisha. Wikipedia notes that the usable part is actually the stem's wood, often called pith.

Sahapedia describes the work. The artisan shaves off the woody outer layer to show the white core. The core is sliced into sheets (kap) or thin strips (paturi). Some pieces are pressed in plaster moulds, then cut into floral or geometric shapes. Designs are carved with a scraping tool and long blades, petals are added and the piece is coloured.

Traditionally it decorated Hindu idols and made the topor, the crown worn by bride and groom in Bengali weddings. Today it also makes home decor, toys, animal figures, flowers and carved panels. Large Kolkata pandals are decorated with it.
artist: The makers are the Malakar, a name linked to 'garland maker'. Sahapedia gives two origin stories: one has the first Malakar born of Vishwakarma and a cursed gopi, Ghritachi (from the Brahma Vaivarta Purana); another says a young man made a white conical hat of shola for Shiva. Many Malakars worship Shiva.
Women play a large part in production. Sahapedia says the craft gives them some economic independence.

Sahapedia also records hardship. Many Malakars take up daily-wage farm or construction work because the craft does not pay fairly, and the next generation has few reasons to stay. Wikipedia says some Kumortuli idol makers now also make sholapith idols, mostly for overseas puja groups.
place: Shola grows in marshes, so the craft lives in rural, low-lying Bengal. Wikipedia lists Bardhaman, Murshidabad, Birbhum, Nadia, Hooghly, Malda and South 24 Parganas as main areas. Murshidabad is noted for floral designs, deity headwear and garlands.
Raw shola is sold in rolls of 20 to 25 sheets at weekly markets. Kolkata is where much of the finished festival work is seen.

history.what: The Malakar association with wedding and temple decoration is described as long-standing. Sources give no firm start date, and we do not give one.
Wikipedia says shola pith helmets were made in India until about this year, and were popular with Westerners in tropical colonies until the late 1960s.
Sahapedia reports that artificial dyes now replace the old herbal red and black colours.

future: Training: apprenticeships so young Malakars can learn carving and design.
Livelihood: link artisans to design buyers and fair-priced markets, beyond festival season.
Materials: protect the marsh habitat where shola grows, and revive herbal colours.
Documentation: record Malakar songs, legends and pattern names.
Protection: shola craft is reported to carry a GI tag, but I could not confirm this from an official page.

name: Sikki Grass Craft
tagline: Golden marsh grass, coiled around a frame of munj, into baskets, boxes and small animals.
facts: Material: sikki grass, with munj grass as the frame
Tool: a slender iron needle called takua
A medium basket can take 8-10 hours to weave
GI tag: sources give different years (2007 and 2018)
art: Sikki is a golden grass that grows in marshy ground in the Mithila region. Meme Raki describes it as harvested in the monsoon and valued for its soft texture and sheen. Sikki is delicate, so artisans build the shape from stronger munj grass and wrap fine sikki strands round it.

The wrapping is done with a thin iron tool called a takua. The coil covers the frame completely, so the piece looks seamless. Down To Earth describes the steps: choose strands that are neither too brittle nor too soft, boil the bundle, dry it in shade, and dye it with colours the artisans often prepare themselves. Some pieces keep the grass's natural gold.

The craft began in the home. Women made baskets, containers, toys and ritual objects for weddings and festivals. Down To Earth notes that sikki vermilion boxes are given to brides in Mithilanchal. Today the range also includes trays, coasters, lampshades and wall decor, and figures of elephants, birds and peacocks.
artist: Sikki has traditionally been women's work, passed from mother to daughter. Down To Earth speaks to a third-generation artisan, Rajesh Kumar, who works with his grandmother, mother, sister and wife. Families do the whole process themselves, from preparing grass to dyeing and weaving.

The work is hard on the body. Down To Earth reports back pain and skin cuts from long hours of weaving, and says treatment is costly. Artisans also say that cheap plastic goods have cut demand and that many have left for daily-wage work in cities.
Rising heat is also named as a problem. The same article says warmer weather makes the grass brittle, so it needs more time to process.
place: Sikki is tied to Mithila, the region of north Bihar around Madhubani, Darbhanga and Sitamarhi. The marshy, wet land there is where the grass grows. Down To Earth notes the grass also grows in the Tarai of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.
In Mithila the craft sits beside Madhubani painting in domestic and ritual life, especially around marriage.

history.what: Claims that the craft goes back to the Vedic period appear in some craft blogs. The Development Commissioner (Handicrafts) site says tracing its history is hard because there is little physical evidence. Sources differ and we do not state an early date.
The craft grew in Mithila homes as women's work for weddings, festivals and daily use.
Down To Earth says Sikki received a GI tag in 2018, alongside makhana and Madhubani paintings. Another source we saw says 2007. We have not checked the GI Registry, so treat the year as unconfirmed.
Down To Earth reports falling incomes, loss of artisans to migration and the effect of climate change on the grass.

future: Training: teach younger family members, and pay for the time spent learning
Livelihood: support for trade-fair stalls and direct sales, which artisans say they were promised
Materials: protect the marshy land where the grass grows, and test ways to work with brittle grass in hotter years
Documentation: record the designs and the wedding uses of sikki boxes
Protection: back the GI tag with real market access, so it helps the maker

name: Tarakasi (Cuttack Silver Filigree)
tagline: Silver drawn into thread-thin wire and twisted into lace, in Odisha's Silver City.
facts: Odia: tara means wire, kasi means design
Material: fine silver wire
Received a GI tag in March 2024
Products include jewellery, boxes, boats and figurines
art: Tarakasi is silver filigree work. In Odia, tara means wire and kasi means design. The craftsperson makes fine silver wire and then twists, flattens and solders it into patterns.

Outlook Traveller describes the steps. Silver is melted in a mould and poured into a narrow tray. It is hammered on an anvil and drawn through a steel plate gauge into thin wire. The wires are then soldered, pressed and flattened, and twisted into designs.

Products include jewellery, boxes and containers, tiny boats and figurines. Designs include flowers, animals, peacocks, the Sun god on his seven-horse chariot and Durga idols. Odissi dancers wear tarakasi jewellery, and the work was once prized as a gift for kings and guests.
artist: The sources we read speak of Tarakasi craftsmen as a group and do not name individuals or give their numbers. We have left names out rather than guess.
The work demands patience and a steady hand. The Odisha State Cooperative Handicrafts Corporation Limited filed the application for the GI tag.
place: Cuttack is called the Silver City.
Cuttack's silver filigree backdrops, called chandi medha, for Goddess Durga are noted by Outlook Traveller as a local specialty at festival time.

history.what: Drishti IAS says filigree jewellery goes back to Mesopotamia, about 3500 BCE.
Outlook Traveller says the craft has existed in Cuttack since at least the 12th century. Other writers say about 500 years. Sources differ.

A government document to the GI registry links the technique with filigree in Arabia, Europe and Scandinavia, spread by trade. Drishti IAS says it likely reached Cuttack through Persia and Indonesia. This is a theory, not settled history.
The craft is said to have had Mughal support and changed as Cuttack changed rulers.
Cuttack Rupa Tarakasi was reported to have received a Geographical Indication tag.

future: Livelihood: link silversmiths to fair, direct markets so that a rise in silver prices does not wipe out their pay.
Training: apprenticeships so that wire-drawing and twisting skills pass on.
Materials: access to pure silver and affordable tools, with hallmarking.
Documentation: record pattern names and the way each is built.
Protection: use the GI to separate hand-made filigree from machine copies.

name: Thanjavur Dolls
tagline: Round-bottomed dolls that sway and nod when touched.
facts: Tamil name: Thalaiyatti bommai (head-shaking doll)
Two kinds: bobble-head and tilting dancing doll
Linked to Serfoji II, early 19th century
Registered as a Geographical Indication around 2008-09
art: Thanjavur dolls are known in Tamil as thalaiyatti bommai. Thalai means head, aatti means shaking, and bommai means doll. There are two main kinds, the bobble-head doll and the tilting or dancing doll.

The dolls are heavy at the base, so they rock and sway without falling. Oaklores says the body is made from a dough of powdered paper (bommai maavu), starch and mud, with copper sulphate added as a fungicide. It is shaped over a paper outline and fixed to a terracotta bowl at the bottom. The doll is then painted in bright colours.

Vajiram and Ravi describe the dancing doll as having four sections, with metal loops inside that let the parts balance on each other. The dolls come as a king and queen pair or as a single dancing girl.
They are also set out in the Navaratri Golu display.
artist: Oaklores says the dolls are made entirely by hand, with no machines. Faces have no fixed design and follow the artist's imagination. Making needs several stages, including painting of the face and costume.
Government schemes and women's self-help groups are mentioned as support for the artisans. Dolls are also made to order.
place: Thanjavur is a city in the Cauvery delta of Tamil Nadu, long a royal and temple town. Hinduism Today says the dolls were historically made from clay taken from the Cauvery banks.
The GI is held by a Thanjavur group. A SpicyIP note on the registration says only the authentic Raja-Rani pair on a curved pedestal may be called the dancing doll of Tanjavur.

history.what: Most sources credit the craft to the reign of the Maratha ruler Serfoji II in Thanjavur. One source gives the 17th century; this is an outlier.
Dolls moved from royal decoration to popular festival use.
The dolls were added to the Geographical Indications Registry. Sources give 2008-09 or 2009.

future: Train new artisans in paper dough work, balancing and painting.
Keep alive the use of local clay and eco-friendly materials against plastic toys.
Support women's groups with materials and loans.
Market the dolls with the story of the maker and the GI.
Document the doll's design and the skills of senior makers.

name: Thewa Jewellery
tagline: Gold lace, cut by hand and fused onto coloured glass, from one small town.
facts: Form: engraved gold sheet fused onto coloured glass
Home: Pratapgarh, Rajasthan
GI tag: 'Thewa Art Work' (sources give 2014; application no. 244)
Traditionally dated to the 18th century; sources differ
art: Thewa is a jewellery craft from Pratapgarh in southern Rajasthan. A very thin sheet of gold is cut and engraved into fine openwork, often in scenes from nature, court life and myth. The gold is then fused onto coloured glass.

IAS Gyan describes the materials as 23-carat gold beaten into a sheet of about 40 gauge, Belgian glass in ruby red, emerald green and sapphire blue, and a silver casing. The page says the gold is joined to the glass by a thermal process with no glue or solder.

Outlook Traveller gives the name as a blend of two Malwa words: one for turning gold into thin sheets, and one for the silver frame of the ornament. A single detailed piece can take up to a month, according to IAS Gyan.
artist: The craft is tied to one family of goldsmiths, the Raj Sonis. Both pages name the goldsmith Nathu Ji (or Nathulal) Soni as the creator of the technique. Outlook says the ruler gave him the title Raj Soni, meaning royal goldsmith.

IAS Gyan says the know-how is guarded as a family secret and passed on by word of mouth in the male line, and that only 14 to 16 families practise it today. Outlook names Raghav Raj Soni as a sixth-generation thewa artist. IAS Gyan says Mahesh Raj Soni received the Padma Shri in 2015.
place: Pratapgarh is a town in the south of Rajasthan, near the borders with Madhya Pradesh. It was the seat of a princely state, and the rulers of Pratapgarh are named as the craft's patrons.
The craft is now promoted as the district's product under the One District One Product scheme, according to IAS Gyan.

history.what: Outlook calls thewa about 400 years old. IAS Gyan gives 1767 in one place and 1707 in another. Other writers give other years. The exact date is uncertain.
Both pages credit a Pratapgarh ruler (named Samant or Sumant Singh) with backing Nathu Ji Soni and giving him the title Raj Soni. Spellings and titles differ between pages.
A postage stamp on thewa was issued, according to IAS Gyan.
IAS Gyan says the GI tag was awarded, registered by the Rajasthan Thawa Kala Sansthan as 'Thewa Art Work'. Other sources give different years.
Mahesh Raj Soni received the Padma Shri, per IAS Gyan.

future: Open up training beyond a few families while keeping the quality that the GI tag protects.
Support apprenticeships so that young people can earn while they learn a month-long craft.
Keep records of designs and methods, with the families' consent.
Use the GI mark to separate hand-made thewa from imitations.
Look for fair prices and direct buyers so the makers keep more of the value.

name: Tripura Bamboo and Cane Craft
tagline: A state with a quarter of India's bamboo stock turns it into baskets, furniture and idols.
facts: About 28 percent of India's bamboo stock (state figure)
19 to 21 species reported
Twenty artisans have won national awards in cane and bamboo
Tripura Bamboo Mission supports the sector
art: Bamboo is part of everyday life in Tripura. Reports list baskets, food grain containers, mats, furniture, lampshades and household goods. News Arena adds uses for rural housing and structural parts, and notes bamboo shoots are a popular food.

The craft rests on a large natural supply. The state says it holds about 28 percent of India's bamboo stock, across about 2,397 square kilometres of bamboo forest, roughly 23 percent of the state's area, with 21 species. The Assam Tribune gives 19 to 20 species. Counts differ by source.
artist: Bamboo is a key forest product for tribal and rural communities. News Arena quotes a department secretary saying its use creates about 6.1 million man-days of work each year.

The Assam Tribune reports that twenty Tripura artisans have won national awards for cane and bamboo craft, though none after 2006. The state set up a Bamboo Heritage Club, described as the first of its kind in India, to honour artisans, especially award winners, and help them train others.
place: Agartala is the centre for markets and training. The Assam Tribune reports a 70-acre bamboo park being built at Bodhjungnagar, about 15 km north of Agartala.
Bamboo grows across the state's hills and villages, so craft is spread widely and not tied to a single town.

history.what: Twenty Tripura artisans win national awards for cane and bamboo craft.
The Bamboo Heritage Club is formed, and a bamboo park is planned at Bodhjungnagar.
The state minister says new technology will be used to raise production and add value, as reported by News Arena.

future: Training: pass skills from award-winning artisans to younger makers, the aim of the Heritage Club.
Livelihood: add value so that artisans' income grows; the Mission aims to double opportunities.
Materials: manage plantations and species well so supply lasts.
Documentation: record artisans, products and techniques by community.
Protection: study GI options; we did not find a confirmed Tripura bamboo GI, so none is claimed here.

name: Varanasi Wooden Toys
tagline: Lathe-turned, hand-painted lacquered toys from the lanes of Khojwa and Kashmiri Ganj.
facts: Made without joints, turned on a lathe and lacquered
Main centres: Kashmiri Ganj and Khojwa
GI: Varanasi Wooden Lacquerware and Toys; sources give 2014 or 2015
Maker community: the Kharadi
art: Varanasi's toys are carved or turned from wood, painted in bright colours and finished with lacquer. The Incredible India page says they are made without joints. Items include animals, figurines, dolls, boxes, bowls and frames.

The steps are: cut pieces from a log, heat slowly to drive out moisture, sand, then shape on a lathe or by hand carving. Several coats of paint follow, then clear or coloured lacquer. Wikipedia says lac is applied by softening a heated lac stick against the spinning toy. Fine lines are painted with brushes of squirrel tail hair.

Wood use has changed. Wikipedia and a New Lines piece say Keria (coraiya) was preferred, but logging limits in the 1980s moved makers toward eucalyptus, which needs more paint. Official pages name sal or sheesham, so sources differ.
artist: New Lines magazine says the toymakers belong to the Kharadi community, whose name comes from kharad, turning wood on a lathe. It says about 3,000 toymakers work in Khojwan, with roughly 200 families doing the whole process. The figure comes from one report.

Craftsmen told journalists their ancestors carved ivory for Mughal and British patrons and moved to wood after ivory was banned. Wikipedia and New Lines both say this, though the ban date is given as 1986 by New Lines.

The New Lines piece names Rameshwar Singh, a national crafts awardee, and Godawari Singh, who it says founded the Khilauna Udyog Sahkari Samiti in 1953. Many kaarigars earn low wages and say they get little credit.
place: The craft is made in the old lanes of Varanasi. Government pages name Kashmiri Ganj and Khojwa as the main centres. Logs are stored outside houses.
Wood arrives from nearby areas, and Wikipedia mentions the forests of Chitrakoot and Sonbhadra.

history.what: New Lines traces the community to this period, as ivory carvers for Mughal and British patrons.
A cooperative society for toymakers is founded, according to New Lines.
Limits on cutting Keria trees move makers toward eucalyptus.
New Lines says an ivory ban pushes carvers to wood.
Artisans apply for a GI tag in 2013. Wikipedia says it was granted in November 2014; the district page lists a certificate date of 30 March 2015.
COVID-19 lockdown nearly halts the industry, says New Lines.

future: Training: government programmes are teaching new trainees, including women, in the craft.
Livelihood: GI and ODOP support have mainly helped master craftspeople; wages for kaarigars need attention.
Materials: a reliable, legal and sustainable wood supply is needed.
Documentation: record designs of the discontinued toy items.
Protection: cheap imports and high electricity costs for lathes threaten small workshops.
